foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: A large cohort study (EPIC-Oxford) found a 30% higher fracture risk among vegans compared with lacto-ovo-vegetarians or omnivores. The same study points to low calcium and vitamin D intake - common when dairy is dropped without a planned replacement - as the likely driver, not veganism itself: this is a reason to make sure you have a planned calcium and vitamin D source, not a reason to worry if you already do.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: open question

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Very high salt intake increases how much calcium the body loses in urine over time; keeping salt moderate protects calcium stores.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Relying on raw oxalate-rich greens alone for calcium gets less of it absorbed than from low-oxalate sources like sesame, ragi or fortified plant milk; blanching helps.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

absorption.text: Vitamin D (mainly from sunlight) helps the body absorb and use calcium; spreading calcium intake across the day, rather than one large dose, also helps.
absorption.label: established fact

protein.text: Dal with rice or roti supplies the everyday protein that bone tissue also needs, alongside a calcium-rich side like til chutney.
protein.label: established fact

preparation.text: Blanching or lightly cooking oxalate-rich leafy greens before eating reduces the oxalates that otherwise bind some of their calcium.
preparation.label: established fact

preparation.text: Dry-roasting sesame seeds or grinding them into a chutney powder (til chutney) is a common, everyday way to include them.
preparation.label: illustration

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Sesame and soy (tofu, soy milk) are recognised allergens; check for a suitable fortified alternative plant milk if either is a problem for you.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: Regular sunlight on skin is the main way the body makes vitamin D; weight-bearing activity (walking, climbing stairs) also supports bone density.
lifestyleLinks.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: A DEXA bone density scan is the standard test for osteoporosis, usually considered for women from their mid-60s or earlier if risk factors are present; a blood test for vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D) is also common.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: Ragi mudde or ragi roti with a spoon of sesame (til) chutney powder and a katori of tofu or soy-based curry - a calcium-forward everyday combination.

redFlags.text: See a doctor if you break a bone from a minor fall or bump, have ongoing unexplained bone or back pain, or notice a loss of height over time.
redFlags.label: established fact

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food can support bone health day to day, but it cannot replace a bone density scan, or the calcium, vitamin D and medication a doctor may prescribe for diagnosed osteoporosis.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A whole-food vegan diet is naturally higher in fibre and lower in saturated fat than one built around refined grains and animal foods, and fibre-rich meals raise blood sugar more slowly.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Fibre and whole grains over refined ones matter most, since they slow how fast carbohydrate turns into blood sugar; regular meal timing and portion size matter alongside food choice.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Stevia (leaf extract) and erythritol (a sugar alcohol) are vegan-compatible, non-nutritive sweeteners that one source describes as not raising blood glucose, unlike table sugar - a practical everyday option for sweetening food or drink without the blood-sugar rise. The same source notes erythritol can have a mild laxative effect for some people at higher amounts, the same caution that applies to other sugar alcohols, and names monk fruit only once in passing as a possible alternative if erythritol doesn't suit someone - without describing monk fruit's own properties, so it isn't included in the claim above.
whatToFocusOn.label: illustration

foodsToFavour.note: 20.4 g fibre per 100 g, among the highest tracked here.
16 g fibre per 100 g, a seasonal Karnataka favourite.
15.6 g fibre per 100 g; a good whole-grain swap for part of the rice portion.
12.6 g fibre per portion alongside protein.
11.6 g fibre per 100 g.
8.3 g fibre per portion alongside protein and iron.
8.2 g fibre per portion alongside iron and calcium.
6.9 g fibre per portion, a whole-grain millet alternative to refined wheat or white rice.
Fibre and omega-3 together; stirring a spoon into a meal can help it feel more filling.
Whole fruit's fibre slows sugar absorption; several studies cited by PCRM link fruit intake with better blood sugar control in people with diabetes - the fruit itself is not something to avoid.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Refined grains (maida, white bread, polished white rice in large portions), sugary drinks and deep-fried snacks are low in fibre and raise blood sugar faster than whole grains and legumes.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Fruit juice removes the fibre that whole fruit has, so it raises blood sugar faster than eating the fruit itself.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Powdered fenugreek (methi) seeds are sometimes suggested as a home remedy for blood sugar, but the dose needed from food alone is too large to be practically effective - worth knowing before relying on it rather than diet and medical care.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Tulsi (holy basil), a traditional herb some readers may take separately as a tea or supplement, may lower blood sugar - combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea medicine specifically, this could cause hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar). Anyone with diabetes considering tulsi should talk to their doctor first, and watch for hypoglycaemia symptoms (shakiness, sweating, confusion) if they do - see this project's own Tulsi herb card for full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Ashwagandha, another traditional herb some readers may take separately, may also lower blood sugar - combined with insulin, a sulfonylurea or metformin specifically, this could cause hypoglycaemia. Anyone with diabetes considering ashwagandha should talk to their doctor first and monitor blood sugar closely if they do - see this project's own Ashwagandha herb card for full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Neem, a third traditional herb some readers may take separately, may also lower blood sugar - combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea specifically, this could cause dangerously low blood sugar. Anyone with diabetes considering neem should talk to their doctor first and monitor blood sugar closely if they do - see this project's own Neem herb card for full detail, including its more serious unrelated cautions (never give neem oil or seed to a child, by mouth).
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Nettle, a fourth traditional herb some readers may take separately, has conflicting evidence on blood sugar (one trial found no effect, another found a benefit in people already on diabetes medication) - but a real case report describes hypoglycaemia in an older adult taking a nettle-containing remedy alongside diabetes treatment. Anyone with diabetes considering nettle should talk to their doctor first and monitor blood sugar closely if they do - see this project's own Nettle herb card for full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Giloy (Guduchi), a fifth traditional herb some readers may take separately, may also lower blood sugar - combined with insulin or other diabetes medicines this could cause hypoglycaemia. This herb also has a separate, more serious documented liver-injury risk unrelated to diabetes - see this project's own Giloy (Guduchi) herb card for full detail before considering it for any reason.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Moringa, a sixth traditional herb some readers may take as a leaf-powder or capsule supplement (separate from eating moringa leaves or pods as an everyday vegetable, which this project's Foods entries already cover), may also lower blood sugar - combined with insulin or diabetes medicines such as glimepiride, glyburide, pioglitazone or rosiglitazone this could cause hypoglycaemia. Worth knowing alongside this: the best current human evidence for moringa actually helping blood sugar is unsettled rather than confirmed, so this caution is about a genuine medicine-interaction risk, not about giving up a proven benefit - see this project's own Moringa herb card for full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Amla (Indian gooseberry), a seventh traditional herb some readers may take as a concentrated extract or capsule (separate from eating fresh amla as an everyday fruit, which this project's Foods entries already cover), has thin and only partly checkable evidence for lowering blood sugar - the single most rigorous cardiometabolic review located for amla did not even test blood glucose as an outcome, and the one review that did gives no effect size to check its finding against. Even so, combined with insulin or another diabetes medicine, any blood-sugar-lowering effect amla does have could add up to hypoglycaemia. Anyone with diabetes considering an amla supplement should talk to their doctor first and monitor blood sugar closely if they do - see this project's own Amla herb card for full detail, including its bleeding-risk and blood-pressure-medicine cautions.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: open question

absorption.text: Eating vegetables and dal alongside rice or roti, rather than a large portion of grain on its own, tends to moderate the overall blood sugar rise from the meal - an idea discussed in one of our cached sources, not independently confirmed here by a government or review source.
absorption.label: illustration

protein.text: Dal with rice or roti is a useful everyday combination: the dal's fibre and protein slow the meal's overall effect on blood sugar compared with grain alone.
protein.label: established fact

preparation.text: Choosing whole grains with the bran intact (whole wheat, millets, brown rice) over refined, polished versions keeps more of the fibre that slows sugar release.
preparation.label: official recommendation

preparation.text: Soaking and sprouting legumes before cooking is a normal home step that also reduces phytates, without removing their fibre.
preparation.label: established fact

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Millets such as bajra, jowar and ragi are naturally gluten-free whole-grain options for anyone managing diabetes alongside coeliac disease or gluten sensitivity.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: Regular physical activity improves how well the body responds to insulin, alongside food choices.
lifestyleLinks.label: official recommendation

lifestyleLinks.text: Poor sleep is linked with harder-to-control blood sugar in general nutrition guidance, though this is a broader observation rather than one specific to vegans.
lifestyleLinks.label: illustration

testsWorthConsidering.text: Fasting blood glucose and HbA1c (average blood sugar over about three months) are the usual tests a doctor uses to check and monitor diabetes.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: A thali with a modest portion of rice or roti, a generous katori of mixed-dal, a large helping of non-starchy vegetable sabzi, and a side salad - balancing the grain portion against fibre-rich dal and vegetables.

redFlags.text: See a doctor if you notice unusual thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, blurred vision, slow-healing cuts, or numbness or tingling in the feet.
redFlags.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Never change or stop a diabetes medicine dose based on diet alone - doing so risks a hypoglycaemic (low blood sugar) episode; any change needs your doctor.
redFlags.label: established fact

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food choices can support better blood sugar day to day, but they cannot replace blood glucose monitoring or a doctor's prescribed diabetes medicine.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A whole-food vegan diet tends to be higher in dietary fibre, which feeds the gut's beneficial bacteria; traditional Indian fermented foods like idli and dosa batter add live cultures on top of that.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Healthy gut bacteria are also linked to gut immune function, not just digestion: one source cites a 2004 study in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition stating that the gut's main antibody (secretory immunoglobulin A, or IgA, which helps protect the gut lining from harmful bacteria) depends on healthy gut bacteria for its production, and a 2003 study in the American Journal of Nutrition stating that without enough beneficial bacteria, certain gut immune cells work less effectively. Separately, it cites a 2008 study in the Journal of Immunology reporting that lactic acid bacteria from fermented foods and drinks generally (not any one specific food) can increase production of anti-inflammatory signalling molecules (cytokines).
whyItMattersForVegans.label: illustration

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Licorice root (Glycyrrhiza glabra), a traditional herb some readers may take separately as a tea, standardised extract or DGL (deglycyrrhizinated licorice) supplement, has a long traditional reputation for heartburn, indigestion and peptic ulcers. The actual trial evidence is real but mixed: a 2011 randomised placebo-controlled trial of a specific low-glycyrrhizin extract (GutGard, not plain licorice) found significant symptom improvement in functional dyspepsia over 30 days, though most of its authors worked for the extract's own manufacturer. For deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) specifically in peptic ulcer, one older uncontrolled survey found healing on endoscopy, while a larger older placebo-controlled trial found no advantage over placebo at all - a genuinely mixed, dated evidence picture, not a settled benefit. This card does not treat licorice as a reliably proven digestive remedy, only as a traditional use with some real but limited supporting trial evidence. See this project's own Licorice Root herb card for full detail, including its separate and much better-established blood-pressure/potassium caution.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whatToFocusOn.text: Fibre (which feeds gut bacteria) and naturally fermented foods (which add live cultures, called probiotics) matter most; variety in plant foods feeds a wider range of gut bacteria.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Onion, garlic and similar vegetables carry a specific fermentable fibre (a prebiotic) that feeds gut bacteria directly, alongside fibre generally.
whatToFocusOn.label: illustration

whatToFocusOn.text: Research cited in one source (Nature, 2012) found that people living in rural West Africa had a more diverse gut bacteria population, including more fibre-loving bacteria, than people in more industrialised areas, whose gut bacteria were dominated instead by strains linked to a diet heavier in meat and carbohydrate. The source reports that Stanford University researchers have proposed regularly eating fermented foods and drinks as one way to help rebuild a more diverse gut bacteria population - a specific, named-study basis for this card's general fibre/fermented-food framing.
whatToFocusOn.label: illustration

foodsToFavour.note: A source of prebiotic fibre that feeds gut bacteria directly, on top of general fibre.
Another everyday prebiotic-fibre source, usually used in small amounts across many meals.
Naturally fermented rice and urad dal batter; fermentation adds live cultures and improves some B-vitamin availability.
Fermented cabbage and salt - always vegan as traditionally made; check the label on shop-bought jars.
A fermented vegetable dish made entirely from plant ingredients - check the label, as some non-vegan versions use a non-plant seasoning.
20.4 g fibre per 100 g, feeding gut bacteria.
15.6 g fibre per 100 g, including fibre types that ferment well in the gut.
12.6 g fibre per portion.
8.2 g fibre per portion alongside iron and calcium.
Fibre alongside omega-3; best ground rather than left whole.
6.9 g fibre per portion as a whole-grain staple.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: A sudden, large increase in fibre or fermented foods can cause temporary bloating or gas; building up gradually and drinking enough water helps.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Many ultra-processed vegan snacks are low in fibre despite being plant-based; whole foods generally do more for gut health than processed substitutes.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Onion and garlic are praised above as useful everyday prebiotic-fibre foods for gut bacteria generally - but for some people they are also a personal trigger for heartburn/acid reflux (GERD) specifically. Both can be true at once: a food can be good for the gut microbiome in general and still be worth moderating personally if you notice it triggers reflux symptoms for you.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

absorption.text: Fermentation itself is a kind of preparation step that improves some B-vitamin availability and reduces antinutrients, rather than a meal-pairing in the usual sense.
absorption.label: established fact

protein.text: Idli or dosa (fermented rice and urad dal) with sambar is a classic combination that already pairs a grain and a dal for everyday protein.
protein.label: established fact

preparation.text: Natural fermentation (idli-dosa batter, sauerkraut, kimchi, dhokla, kanji) grows live bacterial cultures; refrigerating after fermentation slows them down without killing them.
preparation.label: established fact

preparation.text: Soaking and sprouting legumes and grains before cooking reduces some of the compounds that can make them harder to digest.
preparation.label: established fact

preparation.text: The sour taste of fermented foods and drinks is reported to stimulate bitter taste receptors, which in turn trigger digestive secretions - one source cites a 1997 study in the journal Gut showing fermented beverages increase gastric acid output and the release of gastrin (a hormone involved in gastric acid and some pancreatic enzyme production), and a 1999 study in the Journal of Clinical Investigation attributing this specifically to the maleic and succinic acid found in fermented foods and drinks. A specific, named-study mechanism for why a fermented food or drink alongside a meal is traditionally felt to aid digestion.
preparation.label: illustration

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Some people with irritable bowel symptoms find certain high-fibre or fermentable foods (like certain beans) harder to tolerate in large amounts; this varies a lot person to person and is worth discussing with a doctor or dietitian rather than guessing.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: open question

allergensAndSensitivities.text: A small study found that food-elimination testing can meaningfully help people with IBS: of 21 patients following a strict elimination diet, symptoms disappeared for 14; when foods were reintroduced one at a time, the most common triggers found were wheat, dairy products, coffee, tea and citrus fruits. This supports a food-diary/elimination approach to finding personal triggers, consistent with this card's existing advice.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: open question

lifestyleLinks.text: Drinking enough water supports regular digestion, especially alongside a higher-fibre diet.
lifestyleLinks.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: Regular physical activity and adequate sleep are both generally linked with healthier digestion, though neither is specific to a vegan diet.
lifestyleLinks.label: illustration

lifestyleLinks.text: Gut bacteria can take months to recover after a course of antibiotics - one source cites a 2007 article in the International Society for Microbial Ecology journal stating some strains take up to two years to recover, and a 2011 Nature article suggesting some strains may never fully recover. Separately, it cites a 2012 study in the journal Gut reporting that antibiotic treatment can let iron-loving bacteria overgrow in the gut, reducing how much iron the body takes up - meaning an iron supplement taken at that time may partly end up feeding the overgrown bacteria rather than correcting the underlying shortfall. Worth a doctor's input on timing around a course of antibiotics, rather than self-managing.
lifestyleLinks.label: open question

lifestyleLinks.text: Stress is itself a gut-health factor, not just an activity/sleep one: one source cites a 2006 study in the American Journal of Psychology finding that stress can make the gut wall more permeable, raising the likelihood of developing food allergies, and a 2002 article in the journal Gastroenterology reporting that chronic psychological stress is linked to intestinal inflammation.
lifestyleLinks.label: illustration

testsWorthConsidering.text: There is no routine blood test for general gut health; persistent digestive symptoms are usually assessed by a doctor through history, examination and, if needed, targeted tests.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: Idli or dosa with sambar (a mixed-dal and vegetable curry) and a small bowl of coconut-curd-style plant yoghurt - fermented grain, fibre-rich dal and vegetables together.

redFlags.text: See a doctor if you have ongoing abdominal pain, blood in your stool, unexplained weight loss, or diarrhoea or constipation that lasts more than a couple of weeks.
redFlags.label: established fact

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Fermented and fibre-rich foods can support everyday digestion, but they cannot diagnose or treat a digestive disorder - persistent symptoms need a doctor's assessment.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: The body makes all the cholesterol it needs by itself; dietary cholesterol comes only from animal products, so a whole-food vegan diet starts with none of it and is naturally lower in saturated fat.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Low-fat, whole-food plant-based diets have reduced LDL ("bad") cholesterol by about 15-30% across reviewed studies.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Guggul, a traditional Ayurvedic gum-resin herb some readers may take separately as a supplement rather than eat as food, is best known for a researched (though genuinely unsettled) cholesterol-lowering use. A 2021 systematic review pooling 7 trials found an average fall in LDL cholesterol, but a rigorous 2003 US trial in people eating a Western diet found the opposite - no benefit, and a possible small LDL rise, plus a skin-rash side effect in some participants. This card does not treat guggul as a reliable way to lower cholesterol. See this project's own Guggul herb card for full detail, including its thyroid-hormone and bleeding-risk cautions.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Amla (Indian gooseberry), a traditional Ayurvedic fruit some readers may take separately as a concentrated extract or capsule rather than eat as food, has a more consistently positive - though still small and short-term - research base for cholesterol than guggul's. The most rigorous review found (using a stricter risk-of-bias tool, 9 trials, 535 people) found significant falls in LDL cholesterol, VLDL cholesterol and triglycerides, and the single most consistent finding of any amla outcome tested was a fall in hs-CRP (an inflammation marker), with the pooled trials agreeing almost perfectly with each other on that one. HDL ('good') cholesterol and blood pressure did not change significantly in that same review, despite the review's own discussion describing HDL as a significant improvement - an overclaim this project does not repeat. No trial has compared amla directly against a statin. See this project's own Amla herb card for full detail, including its bleeding-risk and blood-pressure-medicine cautions.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Hibiscus (Hibiscus sabdariffa, also called roselle, or sorrel in the Caribbean), usually taken separately as a tea, extract or capsule rather than eaten as food, is best known for a researched - though genuinely mixed - blood-pressure-lowering effect. The largest recent pooled review (17 trials in total across all outcomes, with roughly 11-12 of those - 819 participants - pooled for blood pressure specifically) found a significant fall in systolic blood pressure versus placebo, but no significant fall in diastolic blood pressure, and no significant difference from real blood-pressure drugs in the trials that made that comparison directly; an earlier, more cautious review of just 4 trials concluded the evidence did not support recommending hibiscus for hypertension at all. Hibiscus has actually been tested head-to-head against real ACE-inhibitor drugs (captopril, lisinopril) in at least three trials, with results pointing in different directions across them - roughly equal in one trial, worse than the drug in another, better than the drug in a third. This card does not treat hibiscus as a reliable substitute for prescribed blood-pressure medicine. See this project's own Hibiscus herb card for full detail, including its genuine diuretic effect and its chloroquine-interaction caution.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whatToFocusOn.text: Fibre (lowers cholesterol absorption), plant protein in place of animal protein, and unsaturated fats (nuts, seeds, flaxseed) in place of saturated tropical fats matter most.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

foodsToFavour.note: A strong plant source of omega-3 ALA, plus fibre.
8.7 g omega-3 per 100 g, one of the richest plant sources tracked.
Soy protein has shown LDL-lowering effects in randomised trials cited by PCRM.
A fortified soy milk brings soy protein into an everyday drink.
20.4 g fibre per 100 g, supporting cholesterol excretion.
8.3 g fibre per portion alongside plant protein.
12.6 g fibre per portion.
15.6 g fibre per 100 g, including soluble fibre.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Coconut and palm oil are plant-based but high in saturated fat; the WHO recommends keeping saturated fat under 10% of daily calories.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: official recommendation

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Trans fats, from hydrogenated or partially hydrogenated oils and some fried or ultra-processed snacks, raise LDL cholesterol and are best avoided.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: A large US cohort study (Yang Q, Zhang Z, Gregg EW, 'Added Sugar Intake and Cardiovascular Diseases Mortality Among US Adults,' JAMA Internal Medicine, 2014;174(4):516-524), reported here via a secondary source, found that adults getting 17-21% of daily calories from added sugar had a 38% higher risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than those getting about 8%; above 21% of calories from added sugar, the risk was about twice as high. Not diet-type-specific - about added sugar generally, not tied to vegan vs non-vegan eating, and distinct from sugar naturally occurring in whole fruit or vegetables.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: open question

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Licorice root (Glycyrrhiza glabra), a traditional herb some readers may take separately as a tea, extract or DGL supplement, has a real, well-established mechanism for raising blood pressure: its compound glycyrrhizin blocks an enzyme (11-beta-HSD2) that normally breaks cortisol down in the kidney, letting cortisol act like a sodium- and water-retaining hormone. A 2023 peer-reviewed narrative review found 84 of 104 reported toxicity cases required hospitalisation, with hypertension a leading feature; a US consumer clinical-reference source notes effects can occur with as little as 5 g/day of licorice root in people with existing heart or blood-pressure problems or a high-salt diet, and cites an FDA alert that more than 2 ounces/day of black licorice candy for 2+ weeks may cause dangerous heart-rhythm changes, especially in adults over 40. Anyone with hypertension, heart disease, or taking a blood-pressure medicine, digoxin or a diuretic should talk to a doctor before using licorice root in any form, including DGL. See this project's own Licorice Root herb card for full detail, including its separate pregnancy and kidney/potassium cautions.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

absorption.text: Fibre and plant protein together - for example, a bean-rich meal - lower cholesterol more than relying on just one of the two.
absorption.label: established fact

protein.text: Tofu or tempeh with rice or roti gives a soy-based protein pairing, alongside a fibre-rich bean or vegetable side.
protein.label: established fact

preparation.text: Steaming, baking or pressure-cooking instead of deep-frying keeps added saturated and trans fat down.
preparation.label: official recommendation

preparation.text: Aiming for at least half a cup of cooked beans a day is a simple, practical fibre target.
preparation.label: official recommendation

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (tofu, tempeh, soy milk, edamame) and tree nuts (walnuts) are recognised allergens; those avoiding them can lean more on fibre-rich beans and flaxseed instead.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: About 150 minutes of exercise a week is linked with higher HDL ("good") cholesterol, alongside food choices.
lifestyleLinks.label: official recommendation

testsWorthConsidering.text: A lipid profile blood test (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides) is the usual check; general targets cited are total cholesterol under 150 mg/dL and LDL at or below 100 mg/dL, with a stricter 70 mg/dL sometimes used for those already at high risk.
testsWorthConsidering.label: official recommendation

samplePlate.text: Tofu or tempeh bhurji with a jowar or barley roti and a lobia (cowpea) salad with lemon - plant protein, fibre and minimal added oil in one plate.

redFlags.text: Chest pain or pressure, breathlessness, pain spreading to the arm or jaw, or a sudden irregular heartbeat need emergency care, not diet changes.
redFlags.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Never stop or reduce a prescribed statin or blood pressure medicine because your diet has improved - talk to your doctor first.
redFlags.label: established fact

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food can meaningfully lower LDL cholesterol for many people, but it cannot replace emergency care for a suspected heart attack, or medicine already prescribed for existing heart disease.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A varied, whole-food vegan diet that covers zinc, vitamin D, iron and protein well supports the immune system doing its normal job. The CDC states plainly that vitamin D 'helps the immune system resist bacteria and viruses' and that zinc plays 'an important role in... keeping the immune system strong'. Separately, a deficiency of dietary protein or amino acids has long been known to impair immune function and raise susceptibility to infectious disease, and NIH names 'reduced infection resistance' as a symptom of iron-deficiency anaemia. These four nutrients are exactly the ones a vegan diet needs more planning around (see this project's own zinc, vitamin D, iron and protein cards) - so getting them right is also, specifically, an immune-function point, not just a general nutrition one.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: This is about supporting normal immune function through nutrient adequacy, not about 'boosting' immunity beyond normal. None of the sources behind this card describe a food, nutrient or supplement raising immune function above a normal, well-nourished baseline - they describe what happens when a nutrient is short, and what getting enough of it restores. A reader should come away thinking 'make sure I'm not falling short on these,' not 'eating more of this will supercharge my immune system.'
whyItMattersForVegans.label: illustration

whatToFocusOn.text: Covering zinc, vitamin D, iron and protein well is the main lever here - see this project's own nutrient cards for daily targets, vegan food sources and absorption tips for each. This card does not repeat those targets; it exists to connect them to the immune-function reason they matter.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Vitamin C also matters here - NIH names it directly as helping the immune system work properly - but a vegan diet is not at particular risk of falling short on it (see this project's own vitamin C nutrient card, added specifically to cover this and the iron-absorption link below). It is included in this card's cross-references for completeness, not as a fifth nutrient to worry about alongside zinc, vitamin D, iron and protein.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

foodsToFavour.note: Covers zinc, iron and protein together in one everyday food - already in this project's zinc, iron and protein cards.
A zinc and protein source; calcium-set tofu also covers calcium, useful alongside vitamin D for bone/immune-adjacent nutrition.
Fermented soy - zinc and protein together, already named in this project's zinc card.
High in both iron and zinc per 100 g, among the highest tracked in this project.
A quick-cooking dal with solid iron and protein per katori.
A named zinc source in this project's zinc card.
A named zinc source in this project's zinc card.
An everyday protein source; check the label for vitamin D fortification, since this is one of the main vegan vitamin D routes this project's own vitamin D card names.
A complete-protein whole grain that also contributes zinc.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Phytates in beans and grains reduce how much zinc the body absorbs from them - this project's zinc card already covers this and the soaking/sprouting/fermenting tip that helps. A vegan diet built mostly around unsoaked, unsprouted dried legumes and whole grains, with little variety, is the realistic risk here - not veganism itself.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: More is not better: this project's zinc card already notes that too much zinc from supplements can, over time, lower immunity rather than help it, alongside causing nausea and a copper shortage. A zinc-rich varied diet does not need a separate supplement on top by default.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: A restrictive or poorly planned vegan diet - low in variety, low in overall calories, or skipping food groups - is the real driver of falling short on zinc, vitamin D, iron or protein, not a well-planned vegan diet as such. This mirrors the same honesty pattern this project uses elsewhere: the risk comes from how a vegan diet is built, not from being vegan.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Giloy (Guduchi), a traditional herb some readers may consider for 'immune support' specifically, carries a real, published liver-injury risk with ordinary weeks-to-months self-prescribed use, including documented cases requiring hospital treatment and one death - this is this project's single most serious herb-safety finding. See this project's own Giloy (Guduchi) herb card for the full detail before considering it.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

preparation.text: Soaking, sprouting or fermenting beans and grains before cooking lowers their phytate content and can improve zinc absorption - the same tip this project's zinc card already gives.
preparation.label: established fact

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (tofu, tempeh, soy milk) and sesame, both named above, are recognised allergens; chickpeas, lentils, sunflower seeds or quinoa are reasonable substitutes for zinc/iron/protein if either affects you.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: A thali with masoor dal or chana curry, a side of calcium-set tofu or tempeh, rice or roti, and a fortified soy milk alongside - covering zinc, iron and protein together, with fortified soy milk as one route to vitamin D if the label confirms it.

redFlags.text: This card is about diet supporting normal immune function through nutrient adequacy - it is not a substitute for vaccination, and it cannot treat an active infection. See a doctor for a suspected infection, a fever that doesn't settle, or symptoms that are getting worse rather than better.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: See a doctor if you notice you are getting infections unusually often, infections that take unusually long to clear, or other signs that something beyond ordinary diet and lifestyle may be affecting your immune system - this needs a clinical assessment, not a diet change on its own.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food choices can support the immune system doing its normal job by covering nutrients like zinc, vitamin D, iron and protein - but no food, diet or supplement 'boosts' immunity beyond that normal baseline, treats an active infection, or substitutes for vaccination or a doctor's care.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: For the most common kinds of kidney stones, limiting animal protein (meat, fish, eggs, dairy) and swapping in plant proteins is linked to lower stone risk - a direction a government health body backs directly, not just a vegan-specific claim.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: official recommendation

whyItMattersForVegans.text: One source suggests a specific reason why: vegetarian and vegan eating patterns tend to produce lower urinary calcium and acid, and higher citrate (citrate helps stop stones forming), than diets heavy in animal protein, which push the opposite way. The government source above backs the general advice to limit animal protein, but does not itself spell out this exact urinary-chemistry explanation - so treat the mechanism, specifically, as a single source's illustration rather than an independently confirmed official line.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: illustration

whatToFocusOn.text: If you've ever had, or have a family history of, a calcium-oxalate stone (the most common type), a clinician can set a personal oxalate target for you rather than you following a generic list - most people don't need to cut oxalate-rich plant foods out altogether.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Eat a calcium-rich food at the same meal as an oxalate-rich one, rather than avoiding either. This is the single most specific, actionable tip here - see Preparation below.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Drink enough fluid through the day, and keep sodium moderate - both matter alongside food choice.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

foodsToFavour.note: Named separately by both sources here as comparatively lower in oxalate than most other legumes - a good everyday plant-protein swap for animal protein if you're watching stone risk.

Calcium-set tofu is a plant calcium source named in our kidney-stone book source as a food to pair with an oxalate-rich vegetable at the same meal - the pairing idea itself is government-backed (see Preparation); tofu is one example of a calcium food to use for it.
A fortified, unsweetened soy milk is another everyday calcium source to pair with an oxalate-rich food at the same meal - check the label, as fortification varies by brand.

Named in our kidney-stone book source as a complete, low-glycaemic plant protein that also contains phytic acid, which may help offset oxalate's effect - an interesting single-source lead, not confirmed independently here.

Our kidney-stone book source names fermented soy (tempeh) as lower in oxalate than plain tofu, thanks to fermentation - a specific claim from one source only, worth knowing but not yet independently confirmed.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: If you're prone to calcium-oxalate stones, a government health body names nuts and nut products, peanuts, rhubarb, spinach and wheat bran as foods to limit or avoid, and suggests asking a clinician about other high-oxalate foods for your own personal target.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: official recommendation

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Our kidney-stone book source additionally names beet greens, strawberries and chocolate as oxalate-rich foods worth moderating. Its own list of foods is longer than the government source's - treat these extra items as a single source's lower-confidence addition, not an official recommendation.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: The two sources here don't fully agree on dried beans: the government source names beans, dried peas and lentils generally as lower-oxalate plant-protein options, while the book source separately lists most dried beans (apart from green beans and lima beans) as oxalate-rich foods to moderate. Shown here rather than resolved, since the sources point different ways on this specific point - lentils are the one food both agree is comparatively lower-oxalate.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: open question

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Cooking only reduces the oxalate in a food modestly - our book source puts it at around 15% - so moderating how much and how often you eat an oxalate-rich food matters more than how you cook it.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: This applies to chronic kidney disease (CKD) specifically, not the kidney-stone/oxalate focus of the rest of this card: dried beans and peas, nuts, and several whole grains (amaranth, brown rice, millet, oats, quinoa, spelt) are 'double trouble' foods for CKD - high in both potassium and phosphorus, which a damaged kidney struggles to clear. For someone managing CKD, this source suggests swapping towards green beans or wax beans instead of dried beans or peas, and lower-potassium/phosphorus whole grains such as barley, buckwheat, bulgur, popcorn or wild rice. This is a narrow, CKD-specific caution, not a general vegan one - legumes and whole grains are rightly praised as core vegan protein and fibre staples elsewhere in this project, and that general praise still stands for people without CKD.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Neem, a traditional herb some readers may take separately as a tea, capsule or leaf powder, is rated 'Possibly Unsafe' and might harm the kidneys specifically at large doses or with long-term oral use - a broader caution than, and separate from, the acute poisoning risk in children covered on this project's own Neem herb card. Anyone with existing kidney disease should be especially cautious about taking neem by mouth, and talk to their doctor first.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Hibiscus (Hibiscus sabdariffa, also called roselle, or sorrel in the Caribbean), a traditional herb some readers may take separately as a tea, extract or capsule for blood pressure, has a genuine, reasonably well-evidenced diuretic effect - a dedicated review states plainly 'there is evidence that HS acts as a diuretic,' and separate human trials have found it significantly increases urine volume and raises a kidney-filtration marker (creatinine clearance) compared with placebo. The same review specifically warns against combining hibiscus with the diuretic medicine hydrochlorothiazide, based on animal data suggesting a possible interaction. Anyone taking a diuretic medicine, or with existing kidney disease, should talk to a doctor before combining hibiscus with it, and watch for signs of dehydration or excessive fluid loss if they do. See this project's own Hibiscus herb card for full detail, including its blood-pressure evidence and chloroquine-interaction caution.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Licorice root (Glycyrrhiza glabra), a traditional herb some readers may take separately as a tea, extract or DGL supplement, causes a well-documented kidney-level mechanism called pseudohyperaldosteronism: glycyrrhizin blocks the kidney enzyme 11-beta-HSD2, which normally inactivates cortisol there, so cortisol instead acts on the same receptor aldosterone uses - causing the kidneys to retain sodium and lose potassium, which can lead to hypokalemia, swelling and high blood pressure. A US consumer clinical-reference source lists severe renal insufficiency as a contraindication for licorice, and a German government risk-assessment review notes that because product labels do not state glycyrrhizin content, people with existing kidney disease cannot easily judge their own risk from a given product. Deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) is specifically made to reduce this risk (required to contain no more than 3% of the original glycyrrhizic acid per a Health Canada monograph), but this card's own research found no dedicated kidney-safety data for DGL itself. Anyone with kidney disease should talk to a doctor before using licorice root in any form. See this project's own Licorice Root herb card for full detail, including its separate blood-pressure and pregnancy cautions.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

protein.text: Dal with rice or roti stays a useful everyday combination here too: it supplies plant protein instead of animal protein, which is the main swap this topic's own advice points towards.
protein.label: official recommendation

preparation.text: Eat a calcium-rich food in the same meal as an oxalate-rich one, rather than taking a calcium supplement separately and expecting the same effect. Dietary calcium binds oxalate in the gut before it can reach the kidneys - this is why a government health body says not to cut calcium even while watching oxalate, and recommends getting it from low-oxalate plant foods.
preparation.label: official recommendation

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (tofu, tempeh, soy milk) is a recognised allergen among the plant protein swaps named above; a lower-oxalate legume like lentils, or a fortified alternative plant milk, is a reasonable substitute if soy doesn't suit you.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: A government health body suggests roughly six to eight 8-ounce glasses of fluid a day as a general figure, but says to ask a clinician for the amount that's right for you personally, especially if you've had a particular stone type before.
lifestyleLinks.label: official recommendation

lifestyleLinks.text: Keep sodium under about 2,300 mg a day (roughly one teaspoon of table salt) - this applies even if you're already taking a stone-prevention medicine.
lifestyleLinks.label: official recommendation

testsWorthConsidering.text: If you've had a kidney stone before, a clinician can identify which type it was - calcium oxalate is the most common - since this decides which of the points above matter most for you, rather than following a generic list.
testsWorthConsidering.label: official recommendation

samplePlate.text: Masoor dal with rice or roti, a side of calcium-set tofu or a glass of fortified plant milk, and a cooked (not raw) vegetable sabzi - pairing a calcium source with the rest of the meal, the way the dietary-calcium advice above suggests.

redFlags.text: Sudden severe pain, especially with fever or blood in the urine, or being unable to pass urine, needs urgent medical attention - don't try to manage these with diet alone.
redFlags.label: established fact

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Diet can lower the chance of forming a new stone, but it cannot dissolve a stone that's already there, relieve a sudden attack, or replace a doctor's diagnosis and treatment.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A 2025 systematic review pooling 23 studies and over 700,000 adults found that people eating a healthy, whole-food plant-based diet had lower odds of anxiety, depression and psychological distress than people eating the least plant-based diet, and a lower long-term risk of depression, cognitive decline and dementia. These are associations from observational studies, not proof that the diet caused the lower risk, and they are not a substitute for treatment - but it is a reassuring, well-sized body of evidence for a whole-food vegan diet's role in long-term mental wellbeing.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: The same review found the opposite pattern for an unhealthy plant-based diet - one that cuts out animal foods but relies heavily on refined grains, added sugar and heavily processed plant foods - which was linked to a HIGHER likelihood of anxiety and depression. In short: going vegan on its own is not what the evidence supports for mood; eating mostly whole plant foods is the part that matters.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri), a traditional Ayurvedic herb some readers may take separately rather than eat as food, is best known for memory rather than mood specifically. Two independent systematic reviews/meta-analyses of human trials found real benefits - one for memory free-recall, a later one for speed of attention - though the two reviews point to slightly different specific benefits rather than confirming one single, settled effect. See this project's own Brahmi herb card for full detail, including an important naming caution (it is easily confused with a different plant, gotu kola, also sometimes called 'Brahmi').
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whatToFocusOn.text: Building meals around whole, minimally processed plant foods - vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts and seeds - rather than relying on refined or heavily processed vegan products, since this whole-food pattern is the one the research above actually supports.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: PCRM's Food and Mood guidance highlights three food threads worth including regularly: plant sources of tryptophan (an amino acid the body uses to make serotonin) - PCRM also names watercress, broccoli and pumpkin seeds alongside the foods listed below; ALA omega-3s such as ground flaxseed, chia seeds and walnuts (see our omega-3 nutrient card for how the body converts ALA into EPA/DHA); and antioxidant-rich fruit and vegetables, especially ones containing the plant compound quercetin, which PCRM also names in kale and green tea. Watercress, broccoli, pumpkin seeds, chia seeds, kale and green tea don't yet have their own food cards in this project, so they're mentioned here rather than linked. None of these three threads are proven treatments on their own - each rests on PCRM's own smaller citations, which this project grades cautiously - but they fit naturally into the whole-food pattern above.
whatToFocusOn.label: illustration

whatToFocusOn.text: Many of the tryptophan-rich seeds, legumes and leafy greens named below also appear in this project's zinc, iron and folate nutrient cards - a varied vegan diet that already covers those nutrients well tends to naturally include many of the same foods useful here.
whatToFocusOn.label: illustration

foodsToFavour.note: A leafy green PCRM names as a plant source of tryptophan, the amino acid the body uses to make serotonin.
Named by PCRM as a tryptophan source; also already covered in our zinc nutrient card.
Soybeans are named by PCRM as a tryptophan source, alongside their usual protein and iron content.
Named by PCRM as a tryptophan source among everyday vegetables.
Mushrooms are named by PCRM as a tryptophan source.
An ALA omega-3 source PCRM links to better mood in people eating vegetarian than fish-sourced omega-3 in one small study - also covered in our omega-3 nutrient card.
Ground flaxseed is PCRM's other named ALA source; grinding helps the ALA absorb, as our omega-3 card already notes.
Named by PCRM as a source of quercetin, a plant compound it links to mood via a proposed effect on serotonin-related brain chemicals - an open question, not a settled finding.
Another quercetin-containing fruit named by PCRM.
Named by PCRM for quercetin; onion is already covered in our gut-health card as a prebiotic-fibre food - two separate reasons to keep including it.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: The 2025 review's protective finding was specifically for a whole-food plant-based pattern. A diet that is vegan but built on refined grains, added sugar, white bread, fried snacks and other heavily processed vegan products was linked to a HIGHER chance of anxiety and depression in the same research. Being vegan is not, by itself, the protective part - what you build your vegan diet from is.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: PCRM's own mechanisms (tryptophan, quercetin, omega-3) rest on smaller, single studies - useful context, not proof on their own. Treat them as encouraging background for choosing whole plant foods, not as a diet that will fix low mood by itself.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Shatavari, a traditional Ayurvedic herb some readers may take separately, may reduce how well the body clears lithium - a medicine used for some mood disorders (such as bipolar disorder). This could raise lithium to harmful levels, and a dose adjustment may be needed. Anyone taking lithium should talk to their doctor before trying shatavari - see this project's own Shatavari herb card for full detail, including its own separate, more serious pregnancy-related caution.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Nettle, another traditional herb some readers may take separately, may also reduce how well the body clears lithium, for the same reason as shatavari - a dose adjustment may be needed for anyone taking lithium. See this project's own Nettle herb card for full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

absorption.text: PCRM's handout cites research suggesting a meal higher in complex carbohydrates (vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes) relative to protein makes it easier for tryptophan to reach the brain and support serotonin production, compared with a very high-protein meal. This is a proposed mechanism from a single cited study, not an established population finding like the review above.
absorption.label: open question

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (soybeans) and tree nuts (walnuts), both named above, are recognised allergens; choose another tryptophan or ALA source from this list if either affects you.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: A thali with a spinach or other leafy-green sabzi, a soybean or mixed-dal curry, rice or roti, and a small side of walnuts or sunflower seeds - a tryptophan-rich, whole-food plate built from PCRM's named foods.

redFlags.text: This card is about diet and general wellbeing - it is not a substitute for professional mental health care. If you are having thoughts of self-harm or suicide, call or text the Tele-MANAS national helpline (14416, free, 24x7, in about 20 languages) or seek emergency care immediately. If you notice a sudden, significant change in mood or your ability to function day to day, see a doctor or mental health professional promptly.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If low mood or anxiety is persistent and affecting your daily life - work, relationships, sleep or appetite - see a doctor or mental health professional rather than relying on diet alone. Diet can be a support alongside therapy, medication if prescribed, and a professional diagnosis, never a replacement for them.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food choices may support mood as part of a broader approach to wellbeing, but they cannot diagnose, treat or replace professional care for depression, anxiety or any other mental health condition.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: PCOS is a diagnosed endocrine condition - this card is about how a whole-food vegan diet can support its management alongside medical care, never replace it. Insulin resistance is a central feature of PCOS for many women, and dietary fibre is the clearest, most defensible vegan-diet angle for it: PCRM points to a low-fat, plant-based diet reducing the fat build-up inside cells that interferes with insulin's action, and a real PCOS-specific finding - a fibre-focused substudy of a randomised trial in overweight women with PCOS found increased fibre intake was the strongest predictor of metabolic improvement. An independent, separately found systematic review of dietary fibre and PCOS corroborates this association (reductions in BMI, waist circumference, fasting blood sugar, fasting insulin and HOMA-IR across the studies it reviewed), while honestly noting the exact mechanism isn't yet clear and more research is needed.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: An important honest caveat, not to be skipped: the current international clinical guideline for PCOS (co-developed by ASRM, the Endocrine Society, ESHRE and others) states plainly that there is no evidence to support any one diet composition over another for PCOS's anthropometric, metabolic, hormonal, reproductive or psychological outcomes. So this card does not claim a fibre-rich vegan diet has been proven superior to other diets for PCOS specifically - only that healthy lifestyle and dietary intervention generally is recommended for all women with PCOS, and that fibre's role in insulin sensitivity is well-established general nutrition science this project's own fibre and diabetes cards already cover.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Covering fibre well is the main lever here - see this project's own fibre nutrient card for a daily target and vegan food sources; this card does not repeat those numbers. Omega-3 is a secondary lead: PCRM notes it may help reduce inflammation and improve cholesterol in PCOS, though it adds that more research is needed on dosage - see this project's own omega-3 card.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: This project now has a dedicated magnesium nutrient card (added 31 Oct 2026), resolving the earlier documentation gap - but magnesium is deliberately NOT added to this card's own nutrientIds list below: the only PCOS-specific evidence on file for it is a pooled meta-analysis (magnesium, chromium, zinc, selenium and chromium picolinate together, see the candidateAdditions below) that cannot isolate a magnesium-only effect, which is a weaker, more mixed evidence base than fibre's own PCOS-specific findings. A reader curious about magnesium generally can now be pointed to the magnesium card itself for a daily target and food sources, just without this card claiming a PCOS-specific benefit for it.
whatToFocusOn.label: illustration

whatToFocusOn.text: The international guideline is explicit that there are benefits to a healthy lifestyle even without weight loss, and warns against unduly restrictive or nutritionally unbalanced diets - the same crash-diet caution this project gives elsewhere applies here too. Weight loss, where it happens as part of general healthy eating, has been linked to symptom improvement in PCOS regardless of which diet produced it - this is not a reason to pursue restrictive dieting specifically for PCOS.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

foodsToFavour.note: Fibre, zinc and protein together - already in this project's fibre, zinc and protein cards.
A quick-cooking, fibre-rich dal, already in this project's fibre card.
High in both fibre and zinc per 100 g, already named in this project's fibre and zinc cards.
A whole grain with fermentable fibre, lower-glycemic than refined grains, already in this project's fibre card.
A complete-protein whole grain that also contributes fibre and zinc.
An ALA omega-3 source already named in this project's omega-3 card; best ground for absorption.
Another ALA omega-3 source already named in this project's omega-3 card.

A soy-protein food; PCRM cites a randomised trial finding women who replaced some animal protein with soy protein reduced BMI, fasting blood sugar, testosterone and triglyceride levels - not independently read by this project.
Another everyday soy-protein source, same soy-protein rationale as tofu above.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: PCRM points to limiting high-glycemic-index foods (refined flour, white bread, some breakfast cereals, white rice) in favour of lower-glycemic whole grains and legumes, for insulin sensitivity specifically - worth knowing, but held as PCRM's own illustration rather than an official guideline recommendation, since the international PCOS guideline itself does not endorse one diet composition over another.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Crash or heavily restrictive dieting is explicitly cautioned against by the international PCOS guideline itself, which calls for tailoring dietary changes to food preferences and avoiding unduly restrictive, nutritionally unbalanced diets - the same honesty pattern this project uses elsewhere (mood, skin and hair) applies here: a sudden, severe diet change is the real risk, not whole-food vegan eating as such.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: official recommendation

lifestyleLinks.text: The international guideline recommends lifestyle intervention - exercise alone, or diet combined with exercise and behavioural strategies - for all women with PCOS, to support metabolic health including central body-fat distribution and lipid profile.
lifestyleLinks.label: official recommendation

lifestyleLinks.text: The same guideline names sleep apnoea as a recognised, under-appreciated risk associated with PCOS - worth mentioning to a doctor if you have symptoms (loud snoring, daytime sleepiness, witnessed pauses in breathing during sleep), rather than something to self-assess.
lifestyleLinks.label: official recommendation

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (tofu, soybeans), sesame and tree nuts (walnuts), named above, are recognised allergens; chickpeas, lentils, black gram, barley or quinoa are reasonable substitutes for fibre/zinc/protein if any of these affect you.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: A thali with masoor dal or chana curry, a barley or quinoa portion instead of refined rice, a side of tofu, and a spoon of ground flaxseed stirred in - fibre, soy protein and omega-3 together, built around whole foods rather than refined ones.

testsWorthConsidering.text: PCOS is diagnosed by a doctor, not self-assessed from a symptom list - diagnosis typically involves blood tests (for androgen levels and to rule out other causes such as thyroid problems), a menstrual-cycle history, and sometimes an ultrasound. If you suspect PCOS, see a doctor for proper assessment rather than concluding it from symptoms alone. For the insulin-resistance component specifically, a doctor may check fasting blood glucose, fasting insulin or HbA1c as part of monitoring.
testsWorthConsidering.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: PCOS is a diagnosed endocrine condition. Diet can support its management alongside medical care - it cannot diagnose PCOS, cure it, or replace medical treatment including any medication a doctor prescribes (such as metformin, which the international guideline discusses alongside lifestyle measures). See a doctor for diagnosis, for fertility concerns, or if you suspect you have PCOS - do not self-diagnose or self-treat from this card.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: The international guideline notes PCOS carries a significantly higher prevalence of psychological features (anxiety, depression) alongside its metabolic and cardiovascular risk factors - if this applies to you, it's worth raising directly with a doctor, and this project's own mood and mental health card may also be relevant. See a doctor promptly for very irregular or absent periods, signs of diabetes (excess thirst, frequent urination), or any sudden, severe symptom change.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food choices can support the insulin-sensitivity and general metabolic-health side of PCOS management as part of a broader approach - but no individual food, diet or supplement cures PCOS, and food alone cannot diagnose the condition, resolve fertility concerns, or replace a doctor's prescribed treatment.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A well-planned vegan diet that covers zinc, iron, omega-3, protein and vitamin D well supports normal, healthy skin and hair - this is about supporting that normal function through nutrient adequacy, not about a vegan diet making hair or skin better than anyone else's. See this project's own zinc, iron, omega-3, protein and vitamin D nutrient cards for daily targets and food sources; this card exists to connect them to the skin/hair reason they matter, not to repeat them.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A poorly planned or crash vegan diet - not veganism itself - is the real driver of hair thinning and dull skin. The same honesty pattern this project uses for mood and immune function applies here: a sudden, large calorie cut, cutting out whole food groups without replacing them, or simply not planning what used to come from animal foods (protein, zinc, iron) is what causes trouble, not the decision to eat plant-based. This card should never read as 'going vegan causes hair loss' - that is not what the evidence behind it says.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: illustration

whyItMattersForVegans.text: One genuine, dermatology-sourced incidental benefit worth naming calmly, not oversold: the American Academy of Dermatology's own review of the evidence links cow's milk specifically - not dairy broadly - to higher rates of acne in several large cohort studies (for example, women drinking 2 or more glasses of skim milk a day were 44% more likely to have acne in one 47,355-woman study). The AAD states plainly that no such link has been found for yogurt or cheese, so this is a milk-specific finding, not a reason to think 'dairy-free' alone clears skin - a vegan diet simply avoids milk by default, which happens to line up with this specific piece of evidence. The mechanism is still unclear (a theory involves hormones in milk triggering inflammation), and the AAD itself is careful not to claim settled causation.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Guggul, a traditional Ayurvedic gum-resin herb some readers may take separately as a supplement, has a real but genuinely disputed research link to acne. A small 1994 Indian trial found oral gugulipid reduced inflammatory acne lesions about as well as the antibiotic tetracycline, especially in people with oily skin - but a US consumer reference rates this "Possibly Effective" largely on that one small trial, while a cancer-centre clinical database states plainly that evidence is lacking for guggul alone on acne. This card treats it as an open question, not a confirmed acne treatment. See this project's own Guggul herb card for full detail, including its thyroid and bleeding-risk cautions.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Amla (Indian gooseberry), very well known as a traditional hair-oil ingredient, has thin and uneven evidence behind that specific use - this card is honest about which part of amla's hair reputation is tested and which is folk practice. A single small trial found an ORAL amla syrup improved the proportion of actively-growing hairs in women with female-pattern hair loss over 12 weeks - a genuine, if small and unreplicated, signal for oral amla specifically. No published trial of amla hair OIL on its own was found; the one topical trial located combined amla with several other active ingredients, had no placebo group, and was funded by the ingredient manufacturer, so it cannot show what amla itself contributed. Amla hair oil remains a well-known traditional practice, not a clinically tested one, on the evidence this project could find. See this project's own Amla herb card for full detail, including its bleeding-risk caution.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Gotu kola (Centella asiatica) - the same plant this project's own Gotu kola herb card found is sometimes also sold under the name 'Brahmi,' not to be confused with Bacopa monnieri, the actual Brahmi this project covers in its separate Brahmi card - has 'early evidence' that applying it to the skin helps wound healing, per a US clinical-reference source, with a proposed mechanism of increased collagen production. A dedicated 2022 systematic review, the first of its kind, found only 4 small human trials testing this directly, with different designs and comparators across diabetic wounds, burns, anal fissure and post-laser skin, and its own authors said a meta-analysis wasn't yet possible - a genuinely early, not yet well-confirmed signal, though with real human trials behind it rather than animal data alone. See this project's own Gotu kola herb card for full detail, including its liver and pregnancy cautions.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whatToFocusOn.text: Covering zinc, iron, omega-3, protein and vitamin D well is the main lever - see this project's own nutrient cards for daily targets, vegan food sources and absorption tips for each.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: A real gap worth naming honestly: biotin also comes up often in hair/skin conversations, but this project does not yet have a dedicated biotin nutrient card, so it cannot be given the same daily-target/food-source treatment zinc, iron, omega-3, protein and vitamin D get here. This is less urgent than it might sound - a dermatology review of the evidence states that average dietary biotin intake is adequate in a normal diet, biotin deficiency is rare, and 'severe biotin deficiency in healthy individuals eating a normal diet has never been reported.' The same review and a companion dermatology-journal review both conclude that biotin supplementation for hair/skin/nails is not well supported by large-scale evidence outside an actual deficiency state - so this gap is a documentation one, not a sign that vegans specifically need to worry about biotin.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Zinc specifically: alopecia (hair loss) is a well-known sign of an established zinc deficiency, with hair regrowth occurring once the deficiency is corrected - this is the clearest, most defensible zinc-hair link, and it is about avoiding deficiency, not about more zinc meaning more hair for someone already getting enough. The same review notes that evidence linking zinc levels to the more common, everyday forms of hair thinning (in people who are not zinc-deficient) is inconsistent across studies - so this card does not claim extra zinc will thicken hair in someone whose zinc status is already adequate.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

A zinc and protein source, already named in this project's zinc card.
Fermented soy - zinc and protein together, already named in this project's zinc card.
A quick-cooking dal with solid iron and protein per katori, already in this project's iron card.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Crash or heavily restrictive vegan transitions - suddenly cutting calories, dropping whole food groups, or not deliberately replacing the protein, zinc and iron that used to come from animal foods - are the real, documented risk factor for hair thinning and dull skin, not veganism as such. A gradual, planned transition that keeps calories and these nutrients adequate does not carry the same risk.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Phytates in beans and grains reduce how much zinc the body absorbs from them - this project's zinc card already covers this and the soaking/sprouting/fermenting tip that helps.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Do not expect biotin or zinc supplements, taken on top of an already-adequate diet, to meaningfully improve hair or skin - the dermatology evidence for supplementing beyond normal dietary adequacy is weak, and more is not simply better here.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

preparation.text: Soaking, sprouting or fermenting beans and grains before cooking lowers their phytate content and can improve zinc absorption.
preparation.label: established fact

preparation.text: Ground flaxseed absorbs better for its omega-3 content than whole flaxseed, as already noted in this project's omega-3 card.
preparation.label: established fact

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (tofu, tempeh, soy milk) and tree nuts (walnuts), both named above, are recognised allergens; chickpeas, lentils, black gram, flaxseed or sunflower seeds are reasonable substitutes for zinc/iron/protein/omega-3 if either affects you.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: A thali with masoor dal or chana curry, a side of tofu or tempeh, rice or roti with a spoon of ground flaxseed stirred in, and a fortified soy milk alongside - covering zinc, iron, protein and omega-3 together, with fortified soy milk as one route to vitamin D if the label confirms it.

redFlags.text: This card is about diet supporting normal skin and hair through nutrient adequacy - it cannot diagnose or treat a dermatological condition. See a doctor or dermatologist for sudden or patchy hair loss, a scalp that is painful, itchy, flaking or inflamed, or a skin condition that is worsening or not responding to ordinary skin care.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Hair thinning and skin changes can also come from causes unrelated to diet - thyroid conditions, hormonal changes, certain medicines, stress, or skin conditions like alopecia areata, eczema or psoriasis. If diet changes alone don't explain what you're seeing, or nutrient levels have already been checked and look fine, see a doctor rather than assuming it's a dietary gap.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food choices can support the normal nutrient adequacy healthy skin and hair depend on - but no food, diet or supplement guarantees faster or thicker hair growth beyond that normal baseline, treats an underlying dermatological or medical condition, or substitutes for a dermatologist's diagnosis and care.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: The thyroid needs iodine to make its hormones and selenium to activate them; a vegan on an unidentified salt or avoiding iodised salt can run short on iodine, since most iodine-rich foods are animal-based.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Iodine (mainly from iodised salt for a vegan) and selenium are the two nutrients that matter most for making and activating thyroid hormone.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

foodsToFavour.note: 28 ug selenium per 100 g, one of the better plant selenium sources tracked here.
18 ug selenium and 1.7 mg zinc per portion.
19 ug selenium and 2.6 mg zinc per 100 g.
18.6 ug selenium per 100 g.
3.65 mg zinc per 100 g, supporting thyroid hormone metabolism.
A useful everyday zinc source.
1.3 mg zinc per portion alongside iron.
30.7 ug selenium per 100 g, among the richest leafy sources tracked.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Eating very large amounts of raw cruciferous vegetables (cabbage, mustard greens, cauliflower) can reduce iodine uptake in people who are already low on iodine; cooking largely removes this effect, so cooked crucifers are not a concern for most people.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Very high soy intake alongside low iodine intake has been debated as a possible interaction with thyroid function; the evidence is mixed and this is flagged as an open question rather than a settled finding.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: open question

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Using only non-iodised salt, or rock salt / sendha namak exclusively, removes a vegan's main reliable iodine source.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Tulsi (holy basil), a traditional herb some readers may take separately as a tea or supplement, may lower thyroid hormone (thyroxine) levels and could worsen hypothyroidism specifically - anyone with hypothyroidism is advised to avoid it. This caution is sourced to one clinical-reference site, not independently cross-confirmed by a second checked for this project - see this project's own Tulsi herb card for full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Ashwagandha, another traditional herb some readers may take separately, works the opposite way: it may RAISE thyroid hormone (T3/T4) levels rather than lower them. Anyone on thyroid medicine should talk to their doctor and may need thyroid function monitored with blood tests if they also take ashwagandha - this caution is independently corroborated by three separate sources, including real case reports of thyrotoxicosis that resolved once ashwagandha was stopped. See this project's own Ashwagandha herb card for full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri), a traditional herb some readers may take separately for memory, also appears to RAISE thyroid hormone (T4) - the same direction as ashwagandha, not the opposite direction seen with tulsi. The underlying evidence here is thinner (one animal study found about a 40% rise in mice), but clinical-reference sources still advise anyone with a thyroid condition or on thyroid medicine to use it cautiously or avoid it, and to have thyroid function monitored if they do combine them. See this project's own Brahmi herb card for full detail, including an important naming caution (Brahmi is easily confused with a different plant, gotu kola).
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Guggul, a traditional Ayurvedic gum-resin herb some readers may take separately for cholesterol, also appears to raise thyroid activity - the same direction as ashwagandha and brahmi. A cancer-centre clinical database lists it as able to raise TSH, T3 and T4 on lab tests, and an academic nutrition textbook describes it as showing "strong thyroid stimulatory action" in animal research. Clinical-reference sources advise using guggul only under a doctor's supervision if you have a thyroid condition or take thyroid medicine. See this project's own Guggul herb card for full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

absorption.text: Selenium helps convert thyroid hormone into its active form, so covering both iodine and selenium together matters more than focusing on either alone.
absorption.label: established fact

protein.text: Dal with rice or roti remains a sound everyday protein pairing; this topic has no protein-specific pairing beyond the general one.
protein.label: established fact

preparation.text: Cooking cruciferous vegetables (rather than eating large amounts raw) reduces the compounds that can interfere with iodine uptake.
preparation.label: established fact
