preparation.text: Keep iodised salt away from prolonged heat and add it near the end of cooking, since iodine can be lost with extended high heat.
preparation.label: established fact

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (tofu, soy milk, soya chunks) is a recognised allergen; this is unrelated to the open question above about soy and iodine.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: Managing stress, getting adequate sleep and staying physically active are generally supportive of overall hormone health, including thyroid function, though none of these replace medical treatment for a diagnosed thyroid condition.
lifestyleLinks.label: illustration

testsWorthConsidering.text: A TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) blood test is the usual first check, done when symptoms, family history or pregnancy planning suggest it; free T4 is sometimes checked alongside it.
testsWorthConsidering.label: illustration

samplePlate.text: A mixed-dal sambar with cooked vegetables, a katori of curd-free vegetable curry, and iodised salt used in cooking as usual - no single special dish is needed for thyroid health.

redFlags.text: See a doctor for thyroid testing if you notice unexplained weight change, ongoing tiredness, feeling unusually cold or hot, a swelling in the front of the neck, hair thinning, or a racing or irregular heartbeat.
redFlags.label: established fact

redFlags.text: If you are on thyroid medicine, never change the dose or stop it based on diet alone, and keep a gap between thyroid medicine and iron or calcium supplements as advised by your doctor, since they can affect absorption.
redFlags.label: established fact

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food can help cover iodine and selenium needs, but it cannot diagnose a thyroid condition or replace thyroid medicine and its regular blood-test monitoring.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Whole plant foods - vegetables, legumes, fruit, whole grains - tend to be higher in fibre and water and lower in calories for the same volume than refined or fried foods, which can help with feeling full on fewer calories.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: illustration

whyItMattersForVegans.text: In a small PCRM trial, moderately-to-severely overweight women who cut animal products and minimised added oil lost an average of 13 lb over 14 weeks without counting calories or adding exercise, and had mostly kept it off two years later.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: illustration

whatToFocusOn.text: Fibre and protein together increase fullness per meal; portion size and how processed a food is matter as much as whether it is vegan.
whatToFocusOn.label: illustration

foodsToFavour.note: Fibre and plant protein together for a filling katori.
12.6 g fibre per portion, filling for its calories; about half a cup of legumes a day is linked with weight loss in a cited meta-analysis.
20.4 g fibre per 100 g.
11.6 g fibre per 100 g.
15.6 g fibre per 100 g; a filling whole-grain swap for part of the rice portion.
High in volume and fibre for very few calories.
8.2 g fibre per portion for a leafy green.
10 g protein per half-cup portion, filling without being calorie-dense.
Fibre in a small everyday spoonful adds to a meal's fullness.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Deep-fried snacks, sweets and refined-flour baked goods are vegan but calorie-dense and low in fibre; they are easy to overeat without feeling as full.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Sweetened drinks and fruit juice add calories quickly without much fullness, compared with water or whole fruit.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

absorption.text: There is no specific absorption pairing for weight; the relevant pairing is fibre with protein in the same meal, for fullness.
absorption.label: illustration

protein.text: Dal or tofu with rice or roti, plus a generous vegetable side, is a filling combination that covers protein without relying on refined carbohydrate alone.
protein.label: illustration

preparation.text: Steaming, boiling or light sautéing uses less added oil than deep-frying, which keeps portions filling without extra calories from oil.
preparation.label: illustration

preparation.text: Keeping legumes and vegetables as the bulk of a meal, with a smaller grain portion, is a simple, repeatable way to build a plate.
preparation.label: official recommendation

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Nuts and seeds are calorie-dense in small amounts and are also common allergens (tree nuts, peanuts, sesame); moderate portions matter if relying on them for a weight goal.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: Regular physical activity, adequate sleep and drinking water before a meal are all generally linked with easier weight management, though none of these are specific to a vegan diet.
lifestyleLinks.label: illustration

testsWorthConsidering.text: There is no single lab test for a healthy weight; a doctor typically looks at BMI, waist measurement and overall health together, rather than weight alone.
testsWorthConsidering.label: illustration

samplePlate.text: A plate that is about half vegetables, a generous katori of dal or beans, and a modest portion of rice or roti - filling on fibre and protein rather than on refined grain alone.

redFlags.text: See a doctor for rapid, unintentional weight loss or gain, extreme fatigue, or signs of disordered eating such as skipping meals often, extreme restriction, or an obsessive focus on food and weight.
redFlags.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Avoid very low-calorie or extreme fad diets without medical guidance, vegan or otherwise.
redFlags.label: established fact

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food choices can support a healthy weight day to day, but they cannot replace medical assessment for rapid, unexplained weight change or treatment for an eating disorder.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: This card's 'active people' means someone doing regular structured exercise or training - recreational to competitive - several times a week, the population this project's cached sports-nutrition sources actually studied (athletes, in their own terms). It is not aimed at everyday incidental activity like walking to the shops or taking the stairs; general lifestyle advice on staying active is already covered elsewhere on this project's health topic cards. The distinction matters because the extra nutrient needs described below come from training load itself (sweat losses, extra red blood cell turnover, tissue repair), not from being active in a general sense.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: illustration

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Well-planned vegetarian and vegan diets can meet the nutritional needs of competitive athletes - this is the position of the American Dietetic Association, Dietitians of Canada and the American College of Sports Medicine, the same lineage behind this project's other vegetarian-nutrition position-paper sources. Clinical trials that matched protein intake and training load found plant protein (soy-matched) builds muscle as well as animal or whey protein, and studies comparing habitual vegetarian and non-vegetarian athletes have found no consistent difference in aerobic or anaerobic performance.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: official recommendation

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Training itself raises or adds new loss routes for several of the same nutrients an ordinary vegan diet already needs some planning for - protein and overall energy, iron, zinc, calcium, vitamin D, vitamin B12 and omega-3 fats among them - on top of the usual vegan-planning list. None of this makes a vegan diet unsuitable for an active lifestyle; it means the planning habits this project already recommends matter a little more, and a couple of genuinely vegan-specific points (creatine and beta-alanine/carnosine, see below) are worth knowing about too.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Protein: endurance training needs roughly 1.2-1.4 g/kg body weight/day and strength/power training roughly 1.6-1.8 g/kg/day for the general athletic population. Vegetarian and vegan athletes are advised a further 10% on top of this (roughly 1.3-1.8 g/kg/day), to offset the somewhat lower digestibility of some plant protein sources - met with a varied mix of legumes, soy foods, nuts, seeds and whole grains across the day, with enough total energy intake so protein isn't diverted for fuel instead of muscle repair.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Iron: athletes generally - and vegetarian/vegan athletes especially - sit at the crossing point of several risk factors that can stack: being on an energy-restricted diet, being an adolescent, being female and menstruating, training at altitude, and running (repeated foot strike can rupture red blood cells, sometimes called 'foot-strike haemolysis'), on top of plant iron already being absorbed less efficiently than iron from meat. This compounding-risk picture is independently described in very similar terms by two separate sports-nutrition textbooks in this project, not just one, which is why it's treated as established here rather than a single source's framing.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: A separate, more specific figure is worth flagging as an open question rather than this card's settled guidance: one of this project's cached sports-nutrition textbooks (2013, so flagged for recheck) states that nonathletic vegetarians are advised roughly double the standard iron amount (about 14 mg/day for men, 32 mg/day for premenopausal women) and suggests vegetarian athletes specifically may need even more than that. This differs from both the NIH general-population figures and the ICMR-NIN RDA this project otherwise uses as its main iron figures (see this project's own Iron nutrient card), and it has deliberately not been adopted as a replacement target here - it's shown as a documented alternative viewpoint, not a number to aim for on your own. If iron is a genuine concern, a blood test and a doctor's or dietitian's advice are the right next step, not self-selecting a higher target.
whatToFocusOn.label: open question

whatToFocusOn.text: Zinc and magnesium: both are lost through sweat and urine during training, and plant diets already supply less zinc with lower bioavailability (phytates in grains and legumes bind some of it) than an omnivorous diet. Overt deficiency is rare, but vegetarian, female and energy-restricted athletes are named across sources as the groups most likely to run low - a reason to keep legumes, nuts, seeds and whole grains a regular, repeated part of the week rather than an occasional extra.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Calcium and vitamin D: both matter for everyday bone health and specifically for stress-fracture prevention under repeated training load (common in running, gymnastics, ballet, basketball, volleyball and watercraft sports). A large cohort study (EPIC-Oxford) found a 30% higher fracture risk among vegans compared with lacto-ovo-vegetarians or omnivores, with low calcium and vitamin D intake - common when dairy is dropped without a planned replacement - pointed to as the likely driver, not veganism itself. This project's usual plant calcium sources (calcium-set tofu, fortified plant milk, sesame/til, ragi, calcium-rich greens) and vitamin D routes (sunlight or a supplement) still apply, with a bit less margin for going without a plan.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Vitamin B12: the same universal vegan point as on every other card here (no reliable source without fortified food or a supplement), reinforced for active people because B12-deficiency anaemia specifically reduces endurance and aerobic performance, not just general health - another reason a dependable fortified source or supplement matters, not a reason to need more B12 than any other vegan.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Omega-3 fats: training and competing raise oxidative stress and can trigger exercise-induced inflammation; a lower ratio of omega-3 to omega-6 fats in the diet is linked with that inflammation running less in check. An unsupplemented vegan diet has very little EPA/DHA; where mainstream sports-nutrition sources default to fish oil for this, the vegan route is an algal-oil DHA/EPA supplement, which needs its own evidence rather than inheriting fish oil's - see this project's own Omega-3 nutrient card. Ground flaxseed, chia, hemp and walnuts supply the ALA precursor, which the body converts into DHA only in small amounts.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Creatine is a genuinely vegan-specific point, not an assumption: the body makes some itself, but the rest normally comes from meat and fish, which vegans and vegetarians don't eat - so vegans and vegetarians typically carry lower resting muscle creatine (phosphocreatine) stores than habitual meat-eaters. One practical consequence noted in this project's cached sports-nutrition sources: people who already eat little dietary creatine tend to respond more noticeably to creatine supplementation (in muscle creatine content and short, high-intensity performance) than people whose diet already supplies a lot of it. This card does not give a dose - talk to a doctor or sports dietitian about whether a creatine supplement is worth trying and how to use it.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Beta-alanine, and the muscle compound it builds (carnosine), follows a similar pattern to creatine: beta-alanine is mainly found in meat, fish and poultry, with only trace amounts in plant oils, so vegetarian diets are linked with lower muscle carnosine content than omnivorous diets. Carnosine helps buffer the muscle during very hard, repeated efforts, so this is mainly a consideration for athletes in high-intensity or repeated-sprint sports, not endurance training generally - worth knowing about rather than a reason for concern, and again a 'talk to a doctor or sports dietitian' rather than a self-directed dose.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

foodsToFavour.note: Calcium-set tofu gives protein, calcium and some iron together; soy is also the plant protein most directly shown in trials to build muscle as well as animal or whey protein when intake is matched.
Choose a soy milk fortified with calcium and vitamin B12, and check the label each time you switch brands.
Solid iron, folate and protein in an everyday katori - a practical everyday protein and iron source for regular training.
Iron and protein in a classic Indian combination, useful on a higher-protein training day.
A quick-cooking dal with iron, folate and protein - easy to fit around a training schedule.
A good plant calcium source, useful given the extra bone-stress-injury emphasis on calcium for active people.
Ground flaxseed is a reliable everyday ALA source - pair with an algal DHA/EPA supplement, since the body converts only a little ALA into DHA.
A useful everyday carbohydrate and calcium source; ragi-based meals help meet the higher carbohydrate needs of regular training.
An easy, well-liked potassium source, useful for everyday electrolyte needs and as a simple pre- or post-training snack.
Only brands fortified with B12 help here - check the label; plain nutritional yeast has no reliable B12.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Tea and coffee tannins reduce how much iron the body absorbs from a meal; having them between meals rather than with food matters a little more given the extra iron-loss routes training can add.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Gastrointestinal symptoms (bloating, cramping, nausea, 'runner's trots') are common during hard or endurance training and are triggered mainly by physiological, mechanical and nutritional factors together, not by being vegan - but a high-fibre whole-food vegan diet can make the nutritional factor more noticeable around intense sessions specifically. Dietary strategies that help include eating the pre-exercise meal 2-4 hours beforehand, choosing easy-to-digest, lower-fibre and lower-fat food close to a session, and 'gut training' (gradually practising fuelling during training to build tolerance). This project's own Gut health card covers the general picture; this is the training-specific extension of it.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Under-fuelling - eating too little energy for the training load, whether by accident, deliberate restriction, or disordered eating - is a genuine risk recognised across sports nutrition generally (not specific to vegan diets), described as low energy availability and, if it persists, relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S). It can affect bone health, hormones, immunity and mood in both men and women, and training itself becomes harder to sustain on too little fuel. This isn't a reason to avoid a vegan diet - well-planned vegetarian diets can meet an athlete's increased energy needs - but it is a reason to eat enough, especially if cutting weight or body fat is also a goal.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Hibiscus has a genuine, reasonably well-evidenced diuretic effect (see this project's own Hibiscus herb card) - worth knowing if you train or compete in the heat or sweat heavily, since it adds to fluid and electrolyte loss on top of what training itself already causes. This isn't a reason to avoid hibiscus tea outright, but it's worth mentioning to a doctor if you also take a diuretic medicine or have kidney disease.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Licorice root's well-established mechanism (pseudohyperaldosteronism) causes sodium and water retention, potassium loss and a rise in blood pressure at ordinary tea or supplement doses taken regularly - this matters more, not less, during hard exertion in the heat, when the body is already managing its own sodium, potassium and fluid balance under stress. Talk to a doctor before combining regular licorice use with intense training, especially if you have high blood pressure or heart disease.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Tulsi, guggul and amla all carry a documented blood-thinning/antiplatelet caution on this project's own herb cards (slowed clotting or reduced platelet clumping) - worth knowing for anyone in a contact sport or at higher injury risk, not just before planned surgery, since it could mean more bruising or slower clotting after a knock or cut. This is not a reason to avoid these herbs, but it is worth mentioning to a doctor, especially alongside any blood-thinning medicine.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Mainstream sports-nutrition sources often default to whey protein and fish oil as their go-to protein and omega-3 supplements - neither is vegan. Plant protein blends (pea, soy, rice) and an algal-oil DHA/EPA supplement are the vegan equivalents, each needing its own evidence rather than inheriting whey's or fish oil's: the clinical-trial evidence that matched soy protein against whey or animal protein for muscle building (cited above) is the relevant evidence for the plant-protein swap specifically.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

absorption.text: A vitamin C food in the same meal - lemon, amla, tomato, capsicum or guava - meaningfully improves how much iron the body absorbs from dal, millets or greens, worth a little more attention given training's extra iron-loss routes.
absorption.label: established fact

protein.text: Dal with rice or roti stays a solid everyday protein pairing for active people too. One older sports-nutrition textbook cached in this project still teaches the outdated idea that plant proteins are 'incomplete' and must be consciously combined within the same meal - this card does not follow that framing. The current, better-supported position (already used across this project) is that a varied mix of plant proteins across the whole day, with enough total protein and energy, covers an active vegan's amino acid needs; conscious same-meal combining is not necessary.
protein.label: established fact

preparation.text: Soaking, sprouting and fermenting batters (idli, dosa) all improve how available iron, zinc and calcium are from grains and legumes - the same preparation tips that help any vegan diet matter a little more given training's extra losses of these minerals.
preparation.label: established fact

preparation.text: Around a hard or endurance session specifically, easy-to-digest, lower-fibre and lower-fat food eaten 2-4 hours beforehand reduces the risk of gastrointestinal symptoms during exercise - a useful adjustment on training days, not a change to how you eat generally.
preparation.label: established fact

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (tofu, soy milk, tempeh, soya chunks) is one of the most useful vegan sources of protein, calcium and B12-fortification together, and the best-studied plant protein for matching whey or animal protein's muscle-building effect - a soy allergy or intolerance needs extra planning around these, with a wider mix of legumes, nuts and a pea- or rice-protein blend as alternatives.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Many commercial plant protein powders are soy- or pea-based; a soy and legume (pea, lentil) allergy together narrows the convenient powder options to rice protein blends - whole-food sources (nuts, seeds, grains) remain unaffected and still work well across the day.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: illustration

lifestyleLinks.text: Training increases sodium and chloride losses through sweat, so active people generally have higher salt needs than sedentary people - usually met incidentally through normal meals and everyday vegan sodium sources (table salt, soy sauce) rather than needing a special plan, though heavy or prolonged sweating in the heat is the situation where an electrolyte drink is more often useful.
lifestyleLinks.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: Overzealous plain-water drinking during long or hot sessions, without replacing any sodium, can occasionally lead to exercise-associated hyponatraemia (low blood sodium) - a reason to match fluid intake to actual sweat losses rather than drinking as much as possible 'to be safe', especially on longer endurance efforts.
lifestyleLinks.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: Regular outdoor training is a useful source of vitamin D from sunlight, alongside fortified foods and a supplement where sunlight is limited - the same route as at any other life stage, just with more incidental sun exposure for many active people.
lifestyleLinks.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: A full blood count and a ferritin (iron-storage) test are the usual first checks if fatigue, breathlessness or declining performance raise a question of iron status - the same tests as for anaemia generally, see this project's own Anaemia card.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: A vitamin B12 blood test is worth asking about if a reliable fortified source or supplement hasn't been a consistent habit, especially given B12's specific link to endurance and aerobic performance.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: A vitamin D blood test (25-hydroxyvitamin D) is worth considering, particularly for anyone training mostly indoors or in low-sunlight months, given vitamin D's role in bone-stress-injury prevention.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: For female athletes with menstrual changes, or anyone with a pattern of repeated stress fractures or frequent illness alongside a strong focus on body composition, a doctor may screen for relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) or the female athlete triad - a short, non-threatening questionnaire exists for this purpose, but it is a doctor's assessment to make, not a self-check.
testsWorthConsidering.label: official recommendation

samplePlate.text: Rajma or chana dal with rice, a side of sesame (til) chutney, a banana, and a glass of calcium- and B12-fortified soy milk - together giving protein and iron from the dal-rice, calcium from the sesame and fortified milk, and potassium from the banana for everyday electrolyte needs. A planned vitamin B12 source, an algal-DHA supplement, and - for anyone training hard or in the heat - attention to sodium and fluid replacement still matter alongside this plate; a creatine or beta-alanine supplement is a separate, optional conversation to have with a doctor or sports dietitian, not something any single meal provides.

redFlags.text: See a doctor if you notice unusual tiredness, breathlessness on mild exertion, dizziness, very pale skin and nails, or a decline in performance that isn't explained by training load - these need a blood test, not self-treatment with supplements.
redFlags.label: established fact

redFlags.text: See a doctor about missed or irregular periods, repeated stress fractures, frequent illness or injury, or a strong focus on body composition alongside restrictive eating - these can be signs of relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) or the female athlete triad, which need a doctor's assessment, not a diet change alone.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Talk to a doctor or sports dietitian before starting creatine, beta-alanine, or any herbal supplement - and especially before combining hibiscus, licorice root, tulsi, guggul or amla with a blood-pressure, heart, or blood-thinning medicine, or before relying on them during heavy training in the heat.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: See a doctor about persistent gastrointestinal symptoms during or after training, rather than assuming it is simply normal for an endurance athlete - most cases are mild, but some can be severe enough to need a medical assessment.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food and planned supplements can meet an actively training vegan's higher nutrient needs, but they cannot replace sensible training-load management, enough rest and recovery, or a doctor's or sports-medicine assessment of persistent fatigue, injury, or a menstrual change.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Major nutrition bodies in the same lineage as this project's other vegetarian-nutrition sources - the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and Dietitians of Canada - hold that well-planned vegan and other vegetarian diets are appropriate at every stage of the life cycle, including childhood. But paediatric and nutrition bodies worldwide are genuinely not unanimous on this for children specifically, and the caution is not flat across all ages: a 2023 review of position papers found some bodies (e.g. the Canadian Paediatric Society) supportive, some (e.g. Germany's national nutrition society) advising against a vegan diet for children and adolescents outright, and others - including one international paediatric gastroenterology body's own 2008 and 2017 positions - more cautious specifically for infants and very young toddlers than for school-age children. This card follows the more cautious, planning-first framing throughout, and does not present an unplanned vegan diet as automatically fine for a child of any age.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Children need several nutrients in amounts that scale up with age and growth rather than staying flat - vitamin B12, vitamin D, iron, calcium, zinc, iodine and omega-3 fats among them - and a couple of these, especially B12, have no reliable vegan food source at all without a planned fortified food or supplement, at any age.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A plant-based child's protein needs are generally met on a varied diet with enough calories - the real risk is a diet too low in calories or too reliant on processed foods, not protein from plants as such.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Vitamin B12 needs rise steadily with age (0.9 mcg at 1-3 years, 1.2 mcg at 4-8, 1.8 mcg at 9-13) and has no reliable vegan food source without fortification - a vegan child needs a dependable fortified food or supplement at every age, not just as an infant.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Vitamin D needs (15 mcg/600 IU a day from age 1 onward) are the same as for adults. Sunlight is the main natural route; fortified foods and, especially in low-sunlight months, a supplement are the reliable back-up on a vegan diet, as at any age.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Iron needs by age (7 mg at 1-3 years, 10 mg at 4-8, 8 mg at 9-13, then rising again to 11-15 mg in the teens) are a genuine planning point: plant (non-haem) iron is absorbed less easily than iron from meat, and young children on an unplanned diet are a well-documented anaemia-risk group. See this project's own Anaemia card for the general picture, which this one extends with child-specific detail.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Calcium needs jump sharply with age - 700 mg at 1-3 years, 1,000 mg at 4-8, then 1,300 mg at 9-13 (the same as the teenage figure) - because bone-building speeds up again around the pre-teen growth spurt. Calcium-set tofu, calcium- and B12-fortified plant milk, and calcium-rich greens are the everyday vegan routes to this.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: How efficiently the body absorbs dietary calcium isn't flat across childhood: it is highest in infancy (roughly 60%, independently confirmed from a government food-safety body's own infant-intake calculation), settles to roughly a quarter in adults, and rises again during the pre-teen and teenage growth spurt - one reason the recommended amount jumps at 9-13 years rather than staying flat.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Zinc needs rise from 3 mg (1-3 years) to 5 mg (4-8) to 8 mg (9-13); plant-based diets both supply less zinc by default and absorb what's there less efficiently (phytates in grains and legumes bind some of it), so legumes, nuts, seeds and whole grains need to be a regular, repeated part of a vegan child's week, not an occasional extra.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Iodine needs are 90 mcg (1-8 years) and 120 mcg (9-13) - iodised salt in everyday cooking is the steadiest vegan route, since the plant-based diet's usual iodine sources (seafood, dairy, eggs) are all off the table.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: No official amount exists yet for DHA itself in childhood, but the adequate intake for ALA omega-3 (0.7 g at 1-3 years, 0.9 g at 4-8, 1.0-1.2 g at 9-13) is achievable from ground flaxseed, chia, hemp and walnuts; a vegetarian source for the DHA itself - which the body converts only a little ALA into - is algal oil, a form the US government's own dietary supplements fact sheet names directly as a vegetarian alternative to fish oil. Whether a supplement is worth adding for a particular child is worth asking a doctor, rather than assuming.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Protein needs by age (roughly 13 g at 1-3 years, 19 g at 4-8, 34 g at 9-13) are generally met on a varied vegan diet with enough calories - legumes, nuts, seeds, soy foods and whole grains across the day, rather than any single 'protein food' at every meal.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Choline needs also rise by age (200 mg at 1-3 years, 250 mg at 4-8, 375 mg at 9-13) and matter for brain development, same as in pregnancy. Soy foods, legumes and whole grains contribute some; this is a nutrient worth keeping in mind on a vegan diet rather than assuming it looks after itself.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

foodsToFavour.note: Calcium-set tofu gives calcium, protein and some iron together, and its soft texture suits most children's chewing ability.
Choose a soy milk fortified with calcium and vitamin B12, and check the label every time you switch brands - fortification varies a lot between brands.
A fortified breakfast cereal is a familiar, everyday way to add iron, B vitamins and sometimes vitamin D to a child's morning meal.
A particularly rich leafy green for iron, calcium and folate together.
Good iron, folate and protein in an everyday katori; mash or cook soft for younger children.
Easy to digest and a classic early food in Indian households, with useful iron and protein.
A useful everyday iron and calcium source; ragi porridge (ragi malt) is a traditional soft first-foods option in many Indian households.
Ground flaxseed (not whole) is a reliable everyday ALA source - a small amount stirred into food is easiest for a child.
An easy, well-liked everyday food and a useful potassium source for a growing child.
Only brands fortified with B12 help here - check the label; plain nutritional yeast has no reliable B12.
A good plant calcium source, but best given ground (as tahini) or in a cooked sweet like chikki rather than as whole seeds, which are a choking risk for younger children.

A useful plant protein source as a smooth nut butter rather than whole peanuts, which are a choking risk for younger children - and talk to a doctor first if there's any family history of peanut allergy.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Whole or chopped nuts and seeds, nut butter eaten by the spoonful, whole beans, raw hard pieces of vegetable or fruit, whole grapes or cherries, and popcorn are all named choking-hazard foods for young children by the US government's infant and toddler nutrition guidance - several of them (nuts, seeds, beans) are also named vegan sources elsewhere in this project, so preparation (grinding, mashing, chopping small, cooking until soft) matters as much as the food choice itself while a child is still learning to chew safely.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: official recommendation

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Loading a child's diet with a lot of extra fibre on top of an already varied whole-food vegan diet can backfire: fibre is filling, and too much of it can reduce a child's appetite for the other foods that carry calories, protein, iron, calcium and zinc. There is no single agreed number for how much fibre a child needs - a commonly repeated rule of thumb is roughly 'age in years plus 5 g/day' for children over 2, but a 2023 review found this is only one of several competing formulas with no real consensus, and gives a much broader working range of about 7-19 g/day for younger children and 20-38 g/day for school-age children. Building meals around whole grains, pulses, vegetables and fruit matters more than hitting an exact number.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: open question

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Relying on an unplanned vegan diet without a dependable vitamin B12 source, especially for a younger child, is the single caution every reviewed nutrition and paediatric body agrees on, even the ones that otherwise differ on whether a vegan diet suits children generally - a planned, supplement-aware approach is what every supportive position actually describes, not an unplanned one.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: official recommendation

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Never give neem oil or neem seed by mouth to a child, in any amount. This is a documented, serious poisoning risk, not a general herbal caution - see this project's own Neem card for the full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: official recommendation

absorption.text: A vitamin C food in the same meal - lemon, amla, tomato, capsicum or guava - meaningfully improves how much iron a child's body absorbs from dal, millets or greens.
absorption.label: established fact

protein.text: Dal with rice or roti is a solid everyday protein pairing for children too. Combining proteins within one single meal is not necessary - a varied vegan diet across the whole day, with enough calories, covers a child's protein needs.
protein.label: established fact

preparation.text: Soaking, sprouting (then cooking rather than serving raw) and fermenting batters (idli, dosa) all improve how available minerals like iron, zinc and calcium are from grains and legumes - the same preparation tips that help any vegan diet matter just as much for a growing child.
preparation.label: established fact

preparation.text: Food texture and piece size need to match a child's own chewing ability - mashing, grinding (e.g. flaxseed, sesame into tahini) and cutting food into small pieces, rather than serving foods whole, is how several of this card's own favoured foods (nuts, seeds, beans) are made safe for a younger child.
preparation.label: official recommendation

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (tofu, soy milk, tempeh, soya chunks) is one of the most useful vegan sources of protein, calcium and B12-fortification together for a child, so a soy allergy or intolerance needs extra planning around these - calcium- and B12-fortified oat or almond milk and a varied mix of legumes are the usual alternatives.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Peanut, tree nut, soy, wheat/gluten and sesame are all common childhood allergens and also named foods on this card - talk to a doctor about safe, age-appropriate ways to introduce them, especially where there's a family history of allergy, rather than guessing.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: official recommendation

lifestyleLinks.text: Regular outdoor time helps the body make its own vitamin D from sunlight - useful alongside fortified foods and a supplement where needed, especially in lower-sunlight months.
lifestyleLinks.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: Picky eating is normal and common in young children, and research suggests a child may need 10 to 12 exposures to a new food before accepting it - patience and repeated, low-pressure offering matters more than any single meal.
lifestyleLinks.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: Routine growth monitoring (height and weight against standard growth charts) at check-ups is the usual way a doctor tracks whether a child's diet, vegan or otherwise, is meeting their needs over time.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: A full blood count and a ferritin (iron-storage) test are the usual first checks if anaemia is suspected - the same tests as for anaemia generally, see this project's own Anaemia card.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: A vitamin B12 and vitamin D blood check is worth asking a doctor about if a reliable fortified source or supplement hasn't been a consistent part of a child's diet.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: Moong dal khichdi (soft-cooked rice and dal) with grated carrot, a side of mashed ripe banana, and a cup of calcium- and B12-fortified soy milk - together giving iron, folate and protein from the dal-rice, easy-to-eat texture for a younger child, potassium from the banana, and calcium and B12 from the fortified milk. A planned vitamin B12 source, iodised salt in cooking, and a conversation with a doctor about vitamin D and omega-3 still matter alongside this plate - no single Indian meal supplies all of a growing child's needs on its own.

redFlags.text: See a doctor if a child seems unusually tired, breathless on mild exertion, very pale, or isn't gaining weight or height as expected - these need a doctor's assessment and, often, a blood test, not self-treatment with supplements.
redFlags.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Never give neem oil or neem seed by mouth to a child, in any amount - serious poisoning in infants and small children can happen within hours, and child deaths from neem oil ingestion are documented. See this project's own Neem card.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card does not give supplement doses for children, deliberately - talk to a paediatrician or dietitian about the right vitamin B12, vitamin D or omega-3 product and amount for your child's specific age and needs, rather than using an adult supplement or an adult dose.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: See a doctor before starting any herbal tea, supplement or Ayurvedic preparation for a child, even one that seems gentle or traditional - this project has not reviewed herb safety specifically for children beyond neem's own documented poisoning risk, and traditional use does not by itself mean a herb is safe for a child.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food, fortified foods and planned supplements can meet a vegan child's higher and changing nutrient needs, but they cannot replace routine growth checks, vaccinations or a doctor's assessment of a persistent feeding, growth or health concern.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: This card uses 'older adults' broadly for people from about 50 onward, because that is where several of NIH's own nutrient guidelines actually change - vitamin B12 (NIH's consumer guidance names 50 as the point most people should switch to relying mainly on fortified foods or a supplement) and iron (NIH's own RDA table drops sharply at 51, reflecting the end of monthly menstrual iron loss for most women). A few points sharpen further still from 70 onward - vitamin D and calcium both step up again in NIH's own tables at that point. Everyday usage elsewhere often means 65+ specifically; this card's wider lower bound is a deliberate choice to match where the evidence itself starts changing, not an assumption that one fixed age fits every point below.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Well-planned vegan and other vegetarian diets are appropriate at every stage of the life cycle, including older adulthood - this is the official position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and Dietitians of Canada, the same lineage behind this project's other vegetarian-nutrition position-paper sources and already used on this project's Pregnancy and breastfeeding and Children cards for the earlier life stages.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: official recommendation

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A real and common risk at this age is simply eating less overall - reduced appetite, a duller sense of taste and smell, dental or chewing problems, social isolation, or finding cooking harder - and this applies to older adults generally, independent of diet type. It is not something a vegan diet itself causes, but it does mean that when intake drops, a vegan diet has a smaller margin on a couple of nutrients (B12 chief among them) that have no animal-food fallback to begin with.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Vitamin B12 is the one point on this card that is not really vegan-specific at all: NIH's own consumer guidance tells everyone over 50, regardless of diet, to get most of their B12 from fortified foods or a supplement rather than relying on food-bound B12, because the body's ability to absorb B12 from protein-bound food falls with age (reduced stomach acid, sometimes atrophic gastritis). A vegan who already has a reliable fortified-food or supplement habit is not being asked to do anything extra here - but that habit becomes even more non-negotiable now, since there is no animal-food B12 source to fall back on if it lapses, unlike an omnivore of the same age.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Vitamin B12: NIH's consumer guidance states plainly that people over 50 should get most of their B12 from fortified foods or dietary supplements, because the body can absorb B12 from these forms more reliably than from the B12 naturally bound to protein in food. A separate clinical nutrition textbook independently corroborates the same point with the same underlying mechanism (declining stomach acid reduces how well B12 is released from food protein) and traces it to the same US Dietary Guidelines recommendation. For a vegan, this does not raise the bar further - food-bound B12 was never a reliable source anyway - but it does mean the supplement or fortified-food habit this project already recommends at every age is, if anything, more essential from here on, not less.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Iron: the usual 'vegans need extra iron' caution actually matters less for most people from about 50-55 onward than it did before, not more. NIH's own RDA table drops the target for women from 18 mg/day (19-50 years) to 8 mg/day (51+), the same figure as for men at any adult age, reflecting the end of monthly menstrual iron loss for most women. One reviewed clinical reference source states plainly that men and women over about 55 are generally not considered at risk of iron deficiency, and advises against taking an iron-containing multivitamin by default - only on a doctor's instruction - because excess iron carries its own risks. This is a genuine change in the default advice, not a reason to stop thinking about iron altogether: plant (non-haem) iron is still absorbed less efficiently than iron from meat, so anyone with an ongoing reason to need more (heavy periods continuing, a GI condition causing blood loss, poor overall intake) should still use the usual pairing tips below, and a blood test - not self-supplementing - is the right next step if anaemia is actually suspected.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Calcium: NIH's RDA rises from 1,000 mg/day to 1,200 mg/day for women at 51-70 (men's target stays at 1,000 mg/day until 70), then rises to 1,200 mg/day for everyone from 71 onward. This lands on top of a separate, well-established change: the body's net absorption of dietary calcium is highest in infancy, settles to roughly a quarter in adulthood, and continues to decline further with age - so the same plant calcium sources this project already favours (calcium-set tofu, fortified plant milk, sesame/til, ragi, calcium-rich greens) need to work a little harder from here on, not because they stop working, but because less of what's eaten gets absorbed.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Vitamin D: NIH's RDA rises from 15 mcg (600 IU)/day to 20 mcg (800 IU)/day from age 71. NIH names older adults as being at increased risk of vitamin D insufficiency partly because the skin's own ability to make vitamin D from sunlight declines with age - on top of the usual vegan-diet point that there is very little vitamin D in a plant-based diet without fortified food or a supplement. A separate clinical nutrition textbook reports that up to 30-40% of older adults who have had a hip fracture are found to be vitamin D insufficient - a striking illustration of the stakes here, not a vegan-specific figure (it is not broken down by diet type in that source).
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Protein and muscle (sarcopenia): as people age, the body becomes less efficient at using dietary protein to build and maintain muscle - a change called anabolic resistance - alongside other age-related shifts (insulin resistance, lower activity, more inflammation) that add up to the same effect. A multi-society expert consensus (the PROT-AGE study group) concludes healthy adults over 65 should average at least 1.0-1.2 g protein per kg body weight per day - noticeably more than the general adult 0.8 g/kg figure this project uses elsewhere - rising to 1.2-1.5 g/kg for those who are unwell, and recommends regular exercise (both endurance and resistance/strength training) alongside this, not protein alone. A 2018 systematic review examining this specifically for an ageing population adds a genuine, vegan-relevant nuance: plant proteins generally contain less leucine (an amino acid thought to help trigger muscle protein synthesis) than animal proteins - under about 8% of total protein in most plants versus roughly 8-14% in animal foods - and the per-meal leucine amount thought to matter most in older adults (roughly 2.5-2.8 g) can need a larger portion of a lower-leucine plant food to reach. Soy is the most leucine-rich everyday plant protein and the best-studied in this context; the same review is explicit that whether plant protein alone reliably prevents muscle loss in older adults is still an open research question, not yet settled either way. The calm, practical takeaway: vary plant protein sources across the day (soy foods alongside legumes, nuts, seeds and whole grains) rather than leaning on one type, and spread protein across meals rather than loading it into one.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Fibre and constipation: about a third of adults aged 60 and older report symptoms of constipation, and the US government's own digestive-disease institute names older age itself, low fibre intake, and taking certain medicines or supplements among the risk factors. A whole-food vegan diet's naturally higher fibre is a genuine advantage here - though fibre alone is not the whole story; adequate fluid and staying as physically active as this project's own Gut health card describes also matter.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

foodsToFavour.note: Calcium-set tofu gives protein, calcium and some iron together; soy is also the most leucine-rich everyday plant protein for muscle maintenance.
Choose a soy milk fortified with calcium and vitamin B12, and check the label each time you switch brands.
Easy to cook soft and easy to digest - useful if appetite or chewing has become more sensitive, alongside its protein and iron.
A quick-cooking dal with solid iron, folate and protein in one katori.
A good plant calcium source, best ground into tahini or a chutney powder rather than left whole, which suits denture or chewing difficulty better too.
Iron, calcium and folate together in one leafy green.
Ground flaxseed gives fibre (useful for constipation risk) alongside omega-3 ALA.
A useful everyday calcium source; ragi porridge (ragi malt) is a soft, easy-to-eat option where chewing is harder.
Easy to eat, a useful potassium source, and its fibre helps with constipation risk.
Only brands fortified with B12 help here - check the label; plain nutritional yeast has no reliable B12.
An easy, familiar way to add B12, iron and sometimes vitamin D to a smaller or simpler meal, if appetite has reduced.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Older adults are more likely than younger adults to be on regular prescription medicines for the heart, blood pressure, blood clotting, diabetes or the thyroid - and several traditional herbs reviewed elsewhere in this project carry real, clinically documented interactions with exactly these kinds of medicines, not a folk caution. Guggul and moringa (supplement form) can change how the liver breaks down some statins via the CYP3A4 enzyme; guggul, licorice root, nettle, amla and tulsi can affect blood-thinning medicines, clotting or blood pressure; licorice root can also interact with digoxin and diuretics, with one clinical-reference source specifically naming adults over 40 as more at risk of its heart-rhythm effect from concentrated or candy forms; moringa (supplement form) can reduce how well the body absorbs levothyroxine (a common thyroid medicine); and ashwagandha and gotu kola can add to the drowsiness of sedatives, which matters more wherever a fall risk is already a concern. None of this means avoiding these herbs outright - it means talking to a doctor or pharmacist first about any regular prescription medicine before starting any of them. See each herb's own card for full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Tea and coffee tannins still reduce how much non-haem iron the body absorbs from a meal - less critical than before for most people past midlife now that the default iron target has dropped, but still worth keeping tea and coffee away from meals for anyone who does still have an ongoing reason to watch their iron.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: A smaller appetite or smaller meals, common with age and not specific to any diet, can quietly reduce intake of several nutrients at once rather than just one - a reason foods that pack several useful nutrients into an easy-to-eat portion (this card's favoured foods above) matter more than usual, rather than any single 'problem nutrient' being the whole story.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

absorption.text: A vitamin C food in the same meal - lemon, amla, tomato, capsicum or guava - still meaningfully improves non-haem iron absorption from dal, millets or greens, for anyone who still has an ongoing reason to focus on iron.
absorption.label: established fact

absorption.text: Spreading calcium intake across the day rather than one large dose helps absorption, and vitamin D (mainly from sunlight, or a supplement where sunlight is limited) helps the body use that calcium - both matter a little more now that absorption efficiency itself has declined with age.
absorption.label: established fact

protein.text: Dal with rice or roti stays a sound everyday protein pairing. The one change worth making with age: spreading protein across two or three meals (roughly 25-30 g of protein at each) works better for muscle maintenance than loading most of it into a single big meal, which is a common pattern at any age but matters more now given anabolic resistance.
protein.label: established fact

preparation.text: Soaking, sprouting (then cooking rather than serving raw) and fermenting batters (idli, dosa) still improve how available iron, zinc and calcium are from grains and legumes, the same preparation tips that help at any age.
preparation.label: established fact

preparation.text: Softer textures and finer grinding - tahini or chutney powder instead of whole sesame, well-cooked moong dal, ragi porridge - help where dental problems or reduced chewing ability have made some of this card's favoured foods harder to eat, without losing their nutrients.
preparation.label: established fact

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (tofu, soy milk) is one of the most useful vegan sources of protein, calcium, B12-fortification and leucine together on this card, so a soy allergy or intolerance needs extra planning around these - a calcium- and B12-fortified oat or almond milk, and a wider mix of legumes and nuts for protein, are the usual alternatives.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Sesame is a recognised allergen as well as one of this card's calcium sources; fortified plant milk and calcium-set tofu remain reliable alternatives for anyone avoiding it.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: Regular outdoor time still helps the body make its own vitamin D, though less efficiently than at a younger age - useful alongside fortified foods and a supplement where sunlight is limited.
lifestyleLinks.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: Regular activity that includes both endurance (walking) and resistance/strength work is recommended alongside higher protein intake for maintaining muscle and bone - protein and exercise work together here, neither replaces the other.
lifestyleLinks.label: official recommendation

testsWorthConsidering.text: A vitamin B12 blood test is worth asking a doctor about regularly from this age, given the universal absorption-decline point above - serum B12 alone can miss some deficiencies, and a doctor may also check methylmalonic acid or homocysteine, which are more sensitive to a true shortfall.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: A vitamin D blood test (25-hydroxyvitamin D) is worth asking about too, especially given how common insufficiency is in this age group.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: A DEXA bone density scan is the standard osteoporosis test, usually considered for women from their mid-60s or earlier with risk factors - see this project's own Bones card for more detail.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: If anaemia is suspected, a full blood count and ferritin test are the usual first checks, as at any age - though from this age it is worth a doctor also considering B12 or folate as the cause rather than assuming iron, given the lower default iron risk described above.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: A periodic medicine review with a doctor or pharmacist - covering prescription medicines together with any herbal tea, supplement or Ayurvedic preparation being taken - is worth asking for regularly, given how many of the interactions described on this card involve medicines commonly prescribed at this age.
testsWorthConsidering.label: official recommendation

samplePlate.text: Moong dal and vegetable khichdi, cooked soft, with a spoon of sesame (til) chutney powder stirred in, a small katori of cooked drumstick (moringa) leaves, and a glass of calcium- and B12-fortified soy milk - an easy-to-chew, easy-to-digest plate giving protein, iron, calcium and B12 together. A planned B12 source, a vitamin D conversation with a doctor, and a periodic medicine review (especially before adding any herbal product) still matter alongside this plate - no single meal replaces any of those.

redFlags.text: See a doctor if you notice unusual tiredness, breathlessness on mild exertion, or very pale skin and nails - these need a blood test, not self-treatment with supplements, and from this age are more likely to reflect B12 or folate than iron.
redFlags.label: established fact

redFlags.text: See a doctor about unexplained weight loss, a noticeably reduced appetite, or eating much less than before - this needs an assessment, since it can have several possible causes, not just a reminder to 'eat more'.
redFlags.label: established fact

redFlags.text: See a doctor if you break a bone from a minor fall or bump, notice a loss of height over time, or have ongoing unexplained bone or back pain - see this project's own Bones card for more detail.
redFlags.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before starting any herbal tea, supplement or Ayurvedic preparation, and before starting an iron-containing multivitamin by default - several herbs on this card interact with medicines common at this age, and extra iron is no longer assumed safe-by-default the way it was earlier in adulthood.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Never stop or change a prescribed statin, blood thinner, blood pressure, diabetes or thyroid medicine because of a diet change or a herbal remedy - talk to your doctor first.
redFlags.label: established fact

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food, fortified foods and planned supplements can meet many of an older vegan's changing nutrient needs, but they cannot replace a bone density scan, a blood test, a medicine review, or a doctor's assessment of unexplained weight loss, a fall, or new confusion.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Well-planned vegan and other vegetarian diets are appropriate for every stage of life, including pregnancy and breastfeeding - this is the official position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and Dietitians of Canada, the same lineage behind this project's other vegetarian-nutrition position-paper sources.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: official recommendation

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Needs for several nutrients - iron, folate, vitamin B12, iodine and choline among them - rise in pregnancy and rise again (or stay raised) while breastfeeding; a couple of these, especially B12 and iodine, have no reliable vegan source without a planned fortified food or supplement, so the margin for drifting is smaller now than at other times.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: On the outcomes that matter most, a typical vegetarian or vegan pregnancy is not linked to extra risk: birth weight is generally similar to non-vegetarian norms. Low birth weight has been reported in some macrobiotic populations specifically, tied to low overall maternal energy intake rather than to being vegetarian or vegan as such - macrobiotic eating is a much stricter, separate pattern, not the same as a well-planned vegan diet.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Iron, folate and vitamin B12 needs all rise in pregnancy and stay raised while breastfeeding, to help build the baby's blood supply and nervous system - all three already need some deliberate planning on any vegan diet, and the room for running short is smaller now.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Iodine and choline needs also rise, both specifically tied to the baby's brain development. A reliable DHA source matters too: an unsupplemented vegan diet has almost no DHA, and international expert consensus recommends pregnant and breastfeeding women average at least 200 mg/day of DHA - on a vegan diet, that is best met with an algal-oil DHA/EPA supplement, the vegan-specific source this project's own omega-3 card already names.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Calcium, vitamin D and zinc matter too, though their needs rise less sharply than iron's or iodine's - the same everyday vegan sources that apply outside pregnancy (calcium-set tofu and fortified plant milk, sunlight or a vitamin D supplement, legumes and seeds for zinc) still apply.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

foodsToFavour.note: Calcium-set tofu is a go-to for calcium, protein and some iron in one everyday food.
Choose a soy milk fortified with calcium and vitamin B12, and check the label every time you switch brands.
A particularly rich leafy green for iron, calcium and folate together.
Ground flaxseed is a reliable everyday ALA source - pair with an algal DHA/EPA supplement, since the body converts only a little ALA into DHA.
High in folate, with useful iron and protein, in an everyday katori.
Iron and folate in a classic Indian combination.
One of the better plant calcium sources - close to the tahini (sesame paste) named specifically for pregnancy by PCRM.
A calcium source alongside its protein and magnesium.
A strong vitamin C source - pair with iron-rich dals and greens to help the body absorb their iron.
Only brands fortified with B12 help here - plain nutritional yeast has no reliable B12, the same caveat as elsewhere in this project.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Tea and coffee tannins reduce how much iron the body absorbs from a meal; having them between meals rather than with food matters a little more now that pregnancy raises iron needs.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Leaning on seaweed (kelp, nori) for iodine without moderation can occasionally tip into too much: very high maternal iodine intake from seaweed has been linked to newborn hypothyroidism in Japan and postpartum thyroiditis in China. Iodised salt used in everyday cooking is the steadier, better-studied route to the extra iodine pregnancy needs.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Raw or lightly cooked sprouts - including mung bean (moong) sprouts, a common Indian ingredient - carry a Listeria risk that rinsing does not remove. This project's usual sprouting tip for better mineral availability is best followed by cooking the sprouts rather than eating them raw during pregnancy.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: official recommendation

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Several Ayurvedic herbs used traditionally in India carry their own documented 'avoid in pregnancy or while breastfeeding' caution from clinical-reference sources, independent of whatever benefit they might otherwise offer: ashwagandha, brahmi, giloy/guduchi, guggul, hibiscus (supplements or concentrated extract), licorice root, moringa (supplement form, any part), neem, nettle, shatavari, gotu kola, tulsi, and amla (supplements or concentrated extract only - not the everyday fresh fruit). See each herb's own card for its specific reason and source.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Unripe or semi-ripe papaya is a traditional Indian pregnancy caution. The one controlled study found that papaya latex, concentrated in unripe fruit, caused contractions in an isolated rat-uterus model similar to labour-related hormones, while ripe papaya juice showed no such effect - but this is animal-tissue evidence only, not a human study, so it is included here as a traditional precaution worth knowing, not a settled finding. Ripe papaya itself was not shown to carry this risk.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: open question

absorption.text: A vitamin C food in the same meal - lemon, amla, tomato, capsicum or guava - meaningfully improves how much iron the body absorbs from dal, millets or greens, worth a little more attention now that iron needs are higher.
absorption.label: established fact

protein.text: Dal with rice or roti stays a solid everyday protein pairing in pregnancy and while breastfeeding. Protein needs rise, but deliberately combining proteins within one single meal is not necessary - a varied vegan diet across the whole day covers it.
protein.label: established fact

preparation.text: Soaking, sprouting and fermenting batters (idli, dosa) all improve how available minerals are from grains and legumes - the same preparation tips that help any vegan diet matter a little more here, given pregnancy's higher iron, zinc and calcium needs.
preparation.label: established fact

preparation.text: Washing vegetables and fruit well, and cooking sprouts thoroughly rather than eating them raw, matters more than usual in pregnancy because of a higher Listeria risk.
preparation.label: official recommendation

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (tofu, soy milk, tempeh, soya chunks) is one of the most useful vegan sources of protein, calcium and choline together in a pregnancy diet, so a soy allergy or intolerance needs extra planning around these three nutrients specifically - calcium-set tofu's calcium and choline can otherwise be harder to replace from a single food.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

allergensAndSensitivities.text: A tree nut or sesame allergy rules out almond and til as calcium sources specifically from this card's favoured-foods list - calcium-set tofu and a calcium-fortified plant milk remain reliable alternatives.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: illustration

lifestyleLinks.text: Vitamin D needs in pregnancy and breastfeeding are the same as the general adult amount (15 mcg/600 IU per day) - sunlight remains the main natural route, with a supplement as the reliable back-up on a vegan diet, same as at any other time.
lifestyleLinks.label: official recommendation

lifestyleLinks.text: Zinc absorbs less well from a plant-heavy diet, and pregnancy itself raises zinc needs a little - a reason to keep zinc-rich foods (legumes, nuts, seeds, whole grains) regular, alongside the other planning nutrients on this card.
lifestyleLinks.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: A full blood count and a ferritin (iron-storage) test are usual first-line pregnancy checks, the same as for anaemia generally - see this project's own Anaemia card.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: Thyroid function (a TSH blood test) is sometimes checked in pregnancy, partly because iodine needs rise and thyroid problems can affect both mother and baby - talk to a doctor rather than self-diagnosing from symptoms alone.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: A vitamin B12 check is worth asking about if a reliable fortified source or supplement has not been part of the diet, since low maternal B12 in pregnancy has been linked to a higher risk of certain complications.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: Rajma or chana dal with rice, a side of sesame (til) chutney, a katori of cooked moringa or bathua leaves, a glass of calcium- and B12-fortified soy milk, and a wedge of lemon or a small amla - together giving iron, folate and protein from the dal-rice, calcium from the sesame and fortified milk, extra iron and calcium from the greens, and vitamin C from the lemon or amla to help absorb the iron. A planned vitamin B12 source and an algal-DHA supplement still matter alongside this plate - no everyday Indian meal supplies either of those two on its own.

redFlags.text: See a doctor if you notice unusual tiredness, breathlessness on mild exertion, dizziness or very pale skin and nails during pregnancy or while breastfeeding - these need a blood test, not self-treatment with supplements.
redFlags.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Talk to a doctor before starting any new herbal tea, supplement or Ayurvedic preparation during pregnancy or while breastfeeding, even one that seems gentle or traditional - several commonly used Ayurvedic herbs carry a documented pregnancy caution (see the herbs linked on this card), and traditional use does not by itself mean a herb is safe in pregnancy.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Do not take more than a standard prenatal-level iron or omega-3 supplement dose on your own without medical advice - pregnancy iron needs (27 mg/day) are already higher than non-pregnancy adult needs, and very high doses of either iron or omega-3 carry their own separate risks.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: See a doctor promptly about any new or unusual symptom in pregnancy or while breastfeeding rather than waiting it out - this is one of the situations where self-treatment can cause real harm, and a doctor can check things that diet and supplements cannot.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food and planned supplements can meet a vegan pregnancy or breastfeeding diet's higher nutrient needs, but they cannot replace antenatal checkups, blood tests or a doctor's monitoring of how the pregnancy itself is going.

myths.claim: Foods can be classified as 'acidifying' or 'alkalizing' based on the effect they are claimed to have on the body's overall pH, and a diet with too many acidifying foods (named in this source as meat, fish, eggs, cheese, grains, legumes including soy and beans, and refined sugar) causes a state of body-wide 'acidosis' that is presented as a root cause of a wide range of unrelated conditions - chronic fatigue, depression, tooth decay, eczema, tendinitis and 'rheumatic disorders' among them - correctable by eating more 'alkalizing' foods (named as most vegetables, potatoes, almonds, bananas, avocados) and by taking alkaline mineral supplements.
myths.verdict: Not supported as a general mechanism of disease. The body's own regulation (chiefly the kidneys, with the lungs) keeps blood pH within a very narrow range regardless of diet, so the theory's basic premise - that ordinary food meaningfully shifts body-wide pH - does not hold. Diet can shift urine pH, but that is not evidence of a health effect. Where this claim has actually been put to a scientific test (its cancer-prevention/treatment version), a systematic review found almost no research exists either way, so the honest statement is that this specific health claim is untested and unproven, not that it has been actively disproven study by study. Either way, there is no credible basis for using this framework to avoid foods this project recommends, including soy, legumes and whole grains.

explanation.text: The book states this as a named, central mechanism, not a passing mention: 'the body contains both acid and alkaline substances, and the balance between them is critical to our good health... When there is movement away from this ideal pH, frequently caused by our acid-producing diet and lifestyle, the bodily terrain becomes highly susceptible to disease.' It gives a specific numeric target ('normal pH of blood... is 7.39') and a specific list of foods sorted into 'Acidifying' and 'Alkalizing' categories, along with a recommended alkaline mineral supplement regimen dosed by testing urinary pH with litmus paper.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The claim treats a single mechanism (dietary acid load altering body-wide pH) as the explanation for a long, heterogeneous list of conditions with well-established, unrelated causes - 'chronic fatigue, stress, excessive nervousness, depression, rheumatic disorders, tendinitis, eczema, tooth decay' - the same single-cause-for-many-diseases pattern already flagged in this project's other personalised-diet-theory myth candidates (TCM's 'too yin' vegetable food, ACV's 'acid crystals,' potassium deficiency).
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The book's own food classification is internally inconsistent with how it elsewhere treats plant protein: legumes - including soy, a staple plant protein this project already relies on - are listed under 'Acidifying Foods' alongside meat and fish, while whole grains are also listed as acidifying. This is worth recording for this project specifically: if a reader encountered this book's framework uncritically, it could be read as discouraging tofu, beans or whole grains, which would conflict with this project's own, better-evidenced nutrient and food content.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: Mainstream physiology directly contradicts the mechanism: the body tightly regulates blood pH within a very narrow range (about 7.35-7.45) chiefly through the kidneys (excreting excess acid and controlling bicarbonate in the blood) and the lungs (excreting volatile acid as carbon dioxide), regardless of ordinary diet. A hospital patient-education source states this plainly: 'Your body is a smart machine. It regulates pH very well on its own,' and 'nothing you eat will change your blood pH.' The same source adds that urine pH - the measurement the book's litmus-paper self-testing method actually relies on - 'doesn't signify anything about the quality of your diet', so a shift in urine pH (which diet genuinely can cause) is not evidence of the body-wide 'acidosis' the book describes.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: Where this theory has actually been put to a scientific test, the honest answer is 'barely tested' rather than 'disproven point by point'. A systematic review searching for any randomised or observational study linking dietary acid/alkaline load or alkaline water to any cancer outcome screened 8,278 citations and found only a single qualifying study (which itself found no association, for bladder cancer). The reviewers' own conclusion: 'there is almost no actual research to either support or disprove these ideas,' and 'promotion of alkaline diet and alkaline water to the public for cancer prevention or treatment is not justified.' No equivalent systematic search was found or read for this card's other named conditions (tooth decay, eczema, tendinitis, depression, chronic fatigue); this explanation does not claim those have each been specifically tested and found wanting, only that the theory's basic premise (diet changing body pH) is false and that its most rigorously tested specific claim (cancer) is simply unsupported by research either way.
explanation.label: established fact

myths.claim: Over time, the body's tissues and joints accumulate hard 'acid crystals' - a waste product the book attributes mainly to protein metabolism and ageing - and this buildup is presented as the specific, identifiable cause of arthritis, joint stiffness, muscle cramps and premature ageing. Apple cider vinegar (ACV), the book claims, dissolves these crystals back into solution so the kidneys can flush them out, thereby relieving or reversing these conditions - typically taken as an ACV-and-honey drink three times daily.
myths.verdict: Not supported as a general mechanism for arthritis, joint stiffness, cramps or ageing. 'Acid crystals' depositing throughout the body as a cause of ordinary joint problems is not a recognised mechanism in mainstream medicine. The one genuine crystal-deposition joint disease mainstream medicine does recognise - gout, caused by urate crystals - is a specific, diagnosed condition with its own distinct pattern and cause (the body producing too much urate or clearing too little), not a universal explanation for stiff or ageing joints in general, and nothing in mainstream sources suggests apple cider vinegar dissolves urate or any other joint crystal. Separately, the broader evidence for apple cider vinegar's claimed health benefits (including the anti-inflammatory effect this claim relies on) is judged inconclusive, not proven, by the hospital source reviewed here.

explanation.text: The book states this mechanism repeatedly and names it directly: a section titled 'What Becomes of the Acid Crystals Precipitated in the Body That Age Us?' states 'the answer to premature ageing is unhealthy living and potassium deficiency' and that stiff joints and tough flesh result from these crystals; another section, 'All Through Life You Fight Acid Crystals,' states that 'when body tissues hold all the precipitated acid crystals they can, the crystals then appear in the bursae and the joints of the body, resulting in bursitis and arthritis'; a third, 'Toxic Acid Arthritic Crystals Make Joints Grind,' attributes the grinding sound of a rolled neck directly to crystals deposited on the spine. The book's recommended fix in each case is the same ACV (traditionally with raw honey) cocktail, taken three times daily, which it says allows the crystals to 'enter into a solution and pass out of the body.'
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The same mechanism is extended to muscle cramps ('when precipitated acid crystals get into the circulation of the legs and other parts of the body, they can cause severe cramps') and to general premature ageing and stiffness - treating a single, named, mechanical substance ('acid crystals') as the explanation for several distinct, otherwise-unrelated complaints (arthritis, bursitis, cramps, age-related stiffness), the same oversimplified single-cause pattern as this project's other myth candidates (TCM's 'too yin' vegetable food, the blood-type diet's ABO-linked meat need).
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: Mainstream medicine does recognise a real, narrow case of a crystal-deposition joint disease - gout, caused by uric acid crystals, and a small number of other crystal arthropathies (e.g. calcium pyrophosphate deposition) - but these are specific, diagnosed conditions with known mechanisms and treatments, not a universal explanation for ordinary joint stiffness, arthritis in general, muscle cramps or ageing itself. NIH's own patient page on gout confirms this directly: 'Gout happens when urate, a substance in your body, builds up and forms needle-shaped crystals in your joints,' described as 'a type of inflammatory arthritis' with its own distinctive pattern (flares 'often begin in your big toe or a lower limb') and its own distinct cause (the body making too much urate or clearing too little) - not a generic 'acid crystal' process affecting ageing joints everywhere in the body.
